a new public service can attract fewer users than its organisers expect, even when it addresses a real need. hesitation may arise from practical barriers, unclear information or uncertainty about whether the service is intended for a particular person. encouraging participation therefore requires more than wider advertising. one reason is that potential users cannot easily judge what will happen when they attend. a notice may name an advice session without explaining whether appointments are needed, what documents to bring or whether there is a charge. people who have had a discouraging experience elsewhere may be especially reluctant to risk an unnecessary journey. others may understand the offer but be unable to attend at the advertised time. organisers should first investigate these different barriers. speaking only to current users may produce a positive picture while missing the people who never arrive. short conversations with non-users, conducted through trusted local groups, can reveal whether the main difficulty is information, access or the service itself. the questions should invite criticism rather than assume that reluctance reflects a lack of interest. the response can then be specific. clear examples of who the service can help, practical booking instructions and a low-commitment introductory session may reduce uncertainty. different opening times or an accessible alternative may address physical and scheduling barriers. however, encouraging everyone to attend regardless of need could overload the service, so communication should also explain its limits and direct people elsewhere when appropriate. overall, hesitation is often understandable rather than irrational. organisers can encourage suitable participation by explaining the complete experience, consulting missing voices and changing practical arrangements where evidence shows a barrier. success should mean useful access for the intended users, not simply a larger attendance total.

a practical skill i learned from another person was repairing a punctured bicycle tyre. my neighbour, helen, taught me about two years ago, shortly after i started cycling to work. i had been paying a shop to fix every puncture, so i wanted to handle a simple repair myself rather than stop cycling whenever something went wrong. we worked in her garden on a saturday morning. first she showed me how to remove the wheel and find the hole in the inner tube using a bowl of water. instead of doing everything for me, she asked what i thought the bubbles meant. that small question helped me understand the reason for each step, rather than just memorise a sequence. the awkward part was putting the tyre back. i trapped a section of the tube under the edge, and helen noticed before i inflated it. we took it off again, checked the position and tried a second time. i felt slightly embarrassed, but she explained that checking a mistake was part of learning a safe repair. later that month i had another puncture on the way home. it took me longer than it would have taken a mechanic, but i managed it. the lesson mattered because it gave me useful independence and changed how i ask for help. i now prefer someone to explain a decision and let me try it, instead of taking over immediately. i also remember how patient helen was when i asked the same question twice. she suggested keeping a small repair kit in my bag, but reminded me that some problems still need professional attention. that distinction was useful: being independent did not mean pretending to know everything. it meant recognising a repair i could attempt safely and knowing when to stop.

a quick rough drawing without detailed finish.

a quick summary, “racks proved that everyone prefers cycling”, changes a limited observation into a universal preference and a proven cause. a supported summary retains both outcome and uncertainty. for a cause question, point to the weather qualification rather than the rack location.
a quoted amount needs a decision status and scope
a quoted or summarised judgement can belong to another person.
a rainy scene provides a fresh context for two original emphasis examples. neither a photograph nor an emphatic structure establishes how often an event happens.
a range of colors used by a particular artist.

a range of sentence structures can help express complex meaning, but accuracy and relevance matter. there is no official quota requiring a fixed number of conditionals or relative clauses. use a structure when it communicates the relationship you need, and check that punctuation and reference remain clear.
a ratio and a difference answer different questions
a reading activity starts at ten, continues through eleven and is still in progress at noon: i have been reading for two hours.

a reading question asks for a particular relationship: a reason, a condition, a view or a detail. knowing that target gives rereading a purpose. a timed checkpoint samples how efficiently understanding can be reached; time alone does not establish accuracy or mastery.
a reading scene does not show a completed book
a real condition links demand to a possible response.
a real departure board separates destinations, times and platforms. use that arrangement to understand why changing one detail need not cancel the rest of an announcement.
a real departures hall illustrates travel and arrival planning, not the requirements of a particular examination centre.
a real group-discussion setting supports original examples about requests, viewpoints, reasons and decisions.
a real learning setting makes subsidised training concrete. an effective argument explains who might benefit, how the subsidy could help and what funding trade-off remains.
a real notice provides a setting for a longer practical sentence. the original sentence below is separate from the sign and supplies the wording to retain.
a real rainy-street scene provides a concrete context for changing a construction while keeping its meaning. the sentences below are teaching examples, not quotations from the photograph.
a realistic alternative addresses an identified uncertainty.
a reason explains a judgement; an example illustrates how that reason could operate in a particular situation.

a reason explains a mechanism, consequence or relevant value. an example makes that explanation concrete. a qualification defines where the claim applies; it can make a position more precise without making it indecisive. repeating that something is good adds no new support.
a reason explains how the pattern could arise.
a reason explains the preference or experience.
a reason explains why that judgement is reasonable.
a reason for adopting technology differs from a consequence

a reason question needs an explanation, while a location question needs a place. reading efficiently involves moving between those scales as the question requires. a familiar keyword can locate a candidate section, but its surrounding relationships determine whether it supplies the answer.

a reason supports a judgement. a mechanism explains how the proposed effect could happen. an example makes the explanation concrete; it is not a substitute for it. a condition identifies when a claim applies rather than avoiding a decision.
a reason supports or qualifies the option using a relevant concern.
a reasoned case for a particular viewpoint.

a recipe tried slowly develops the available-time reason. the other details need a new connection that the answer has not established. relevance is the check; an impressive vocabulary item does not make an unrelated detail useful.

a recommendation to record surroundings preserves the method’s usefulness while accounting for conditions. it is not equivalent to rejecting rooftop data. a purpose question about strong winds asks how that detail supports the explanation; a main-idea question asks how the whole argument connects observation and practical response.
a record covering the outcome the study is trying to establish
a record of events in a system.
a recorded three times as many visits as b, or three times b's figure. a recorded 60 more visits. these express different aspects of the same data.
a recording and self-review provide useful evidence, but official scoring requires a validated assessment process.
a recording says ‘headphones are not supplied, although microphones are available.’ what should a participant bring?
a red fruit filled with edible seeds.
a red juicy fruit used as a vegetable.
a reference expression needs a recoverable meaning.
a reference keeps one proposal visible across sentences
a reference phrase can point to a whole event

a reference to a classmate should do reasoning work. ‘rosa is right’ alone supplies agreement; the because-clause explains its relevance. a useful concession can lead to a design condition instead of a contradiction. review whether the final judgement remains identifiable after acknowledging a cost.
a reference to a legal authority.
a reference to a source of information.
a reference to an external source
a reference word points to an identifiable entity or idea.

a registered student is free on thursday. what does the announcement require them to do? check: no new registration is specified; the existing one remains valid. they should attend at the new room and date.
a regular article by a specific writer.
a regular journey between home and work
a regular pattern of beats in music or movement.
a regularly updated website or web page.

a rehearsal series rises from 70 to 91 requests. completed calculation: 91 minus 70 = 21. verb frame: “requests increased by 21 to 91.” noun frame: “there was an increase of 21 in requests.” do not mix the finite verb with the noun article.

a reimbursement message travel claims must include a receipt and a brief explanation of the work purpose. submit them within thirty days of the journey. a manager’s prior permission to travel does not replace the claim form. finance staff may request clarification before payment, so complete records can reduce delays without guaranteeing immediate reimbursement.
a relationship is not enough to establish a unique cause. use the author’s qualifications when interpreting the result.
a relative clause adds information without replacing the main assertion.

a relative clause can describe a noun without becoming the main assertion. agreement follows the relevant subject head. word forms must also fit their sentence jobs, so arranging a grammatical sentence involves relationships between phrases rather than simply placing familiar words next to one another.

a relative clause can identify a group: ‘students who work during the day may need evening sessions.’ who refers to students, and work agrees with them. if a sentence becomes overloaded, split it before adding another clause. a clear sequence of controlled sentences can express more range than one long sentence with uncertain boundaries.
a relative clause can identify which people the message concerns.

a relative clause gives more information about a noun in the main clause. the relative pronoun introduces the relative clause and refers back to the noun (the antecedent). choose the pronoun based on whether the antecedent is a person, thing, place, time, or reason.
a relative clause identifies or describes a referent.

a relative clause identifies or describes; a condition restricts a result; a concessive clause introduces a contrast with expectations. control includes completeness, reference and agreement. complexity becomes useful when the structure communicates an intended relationship clearly, rather than merely increasing sentence length.
a relevant answer responds to the question and develops the speaker’s own experience, opinion or reasoning.
a relevant detail develops a personal answer
a relevant direct answer plus a concrete reason and example produces useful interview development; delivery needs spoken evidence.
a relevant spoken answer can expand through a reason and a specific detail while keeping the original question in focus.
a reliable service can be infrequent; a frequent one can be unreliable.
a relief print made from an engraved wooden block.

a remembered answer may depend on familiarity with that item. a fresh sentence or task tests whether the underlying relationship can be reconstructed. reflection becomes useful when it identifies a specific remaining gap and connects it to further practice.

a reminder can state the date, place and a confirmation route together. its success would still depend on people receiving and understanding it, and on confusion actually being a relevant cause. a better-looking notice alone does not prove the problem is solved.
a renewal is automatic even when another person has reserved the item.
a repair centre is worth testing before a large commitment.
a repair club should prioritise the number of completed jobs over explanation.
a repeating natural system contains connected pathways rather than one final manufactured product. the illustration is not a record of the lesson’s fictional experiment.
a replacement preserves participants, timing and event status as well as grammar.
a replacement questionnaire for every student
a report is organised well but confuses percentage points with relative change. what should the next short review test?
a report on a lecture that was not supplied
a report says “the new route is proposed.” can this become “the new route operates daily” without further evidence?

a report states that an intervention was associated with fewer absences. it also notes that staffing and reporting procedures changed during the same period. the association is worth investigating, but the report does not identify a single proven cause. removing that qualification would make the summary less accurate.

a report to the pool manager can use headings such as purpose, findings and recommendations. draft finding: “new visitors cannot easily identify the locker payment process.” add evidence without exaggeration: “during the visit, i needed reception assistance.” action: “place a short illustrated instruction beside the lockers.” review: “ask reception to record related questions for the following month.”
a reported bug or feature request.
a reported view is not automatically the writer’s view
a reporter's assigned geographic coverage area.
a reporting verb can describe tentative support.
a request connects a problem to a useful response
a request for a higher court review.
a request should explain the issue, provide actionable details and say what response is needed.
a request to change a verdict
a requested change may depend on supervisor availability
a required course for all students.
a required minimum of certain content.
a requirement can explain why a preference changes.
a research noun does not supply an unstated result
a researcher checks figures and then revises a report.
a reservation will be made. the exchange does not establish that the book is available immediately.
a residential area near the edge of a city
a response addresses that communicative action.
a response answers a speaker’s communicative action
a response fulfils a prompt when its content performs the actions the situation requires.
a result describes the particular tasks attempted.
a result or effect of an action.
a retired professor with honorary title.
a reusable block of code for a task.
a reusable platform for building applications.

a review evaluates an experience and recommends it to a reader. a report presents findings and practical recommendations for a stated audience; headings can make its structure clear. both require reasons and relevant detail. avoid labelling a response “high band” without examiner evidence. in b2 first, write 140–190 words.
a review evaluates an experience for a reader; a report presents findings and recommendations for a stated audience.
a review identifies what the learner’s work shows, what remains uncertain and which concept needs further application.

a review might evaluate whether the layout suits a small group. a report could recommend more accessible spacing if an inspection found a problem. the first supports a customer’s choice; the second connects a proposed action to findings.
a revised actual response can be compared against specific feedback; xp and memorisation do not establish proficiency.
a revolutionary gene-editing tool that allows precise modification of dna sequences.
a roadside bus shelter has seats and display panels. a large yellow bus stop marking lies on the road, with buildings across the street.
a room booking as complete machine authorisation
a room booking authorises use of every machine.
a room equipped for preparing and cooking food.
a room for scientific experiments and research.
a room or building for displaying art to the public.
a room where teaching and learning take place.

a room-booking notice study rooms may be reserved for up to two hours. a booking is held for ten minutes after its start time; after that, staff may give the room to another user. students must confirm their reservation through the email link. an unconfirmed request does not reserve a room. the system improves access only if users follow the confirmation and cancellation rules.
a rose from 20 to 30 while b stayed at 40 → a increased, but b remained higher.
a round beige legume used in mediterranean cuisine.
a round brown nut with a sweet flavor.
a round citrus fruit with sweet juicy segments.
a round crisp fruit with red or green skin.
a round dark red root vegetable eaten cooked or raw.
a rousing or uplifting song identified with a group.

a route combines a starting location, orientation and a sequence of movements or landmarks. opposite describes a relationship across a space; past describes movement beyond a point. a named facility identifies a place, while the route determines which position is being described.

a route worth exploring do your weekends always look the same? mine did until i joined a walking group that explores overlooked parts of our town. i expected exercise, but i also found stories hidden in ordinary streets. you do not need special equipment or expert knowledge to join us; curiosity and comfortable shoes are enough.
a row of electronic railway departure screens hangs beneath a station roof. the screens arrange service information into repeated columns; a café sign is below them.
a rubber teat for a baby to suck on
a rule about using new vocabulary only
a rule issued by an administrative agency.
a rule’s exception has its own scope
a run-on sentence incorrectly joins independent clauses without conjunctions or punctuation.
a sample of a media product.
a sauce added to salads for flavor.
a sauce of basil garlic pine nuts and oil.
a sauce or seasoning added to food for flavor.
a savory custard tart baked with fillings.
a savory liquid made by simmering meat and vegetables.
a savory sauce made from meat cooking juices.
a says the towpath remained fenced off and residents had no continuous route.
a schedule separates a conflict from an accepted alternative
a scheduled television or radio show.
a school for specialized training or higher learning.
a school lends laptops; demand rises, repairs increase, and lending is reviewed. write one main-idea sentence.
a school specializing in music and performing arts.
a score indicating academic performance level.
a script written for a film including dialogue.
a sculptural technique where forms project from a background.
a season of helping taught the responsibility.
a seasoned mixture stuffed inside poultry.
a seating area can be evaluated for visitors or examined for a manager. the same visible setting does not require the same organisation or conclusion.
a second attempt at a failed exam.

a second construction starts “it was such a noisy room that we moved outside.” such modifies a noun phrase: such + a/an + adjective + singular countable noun. compare so + adjective: “the room was so noisy that...”. practise with “the task was so difficult that we asked for help” → “it was ___ that we asked for help.” include such.
a secondary angle in a news story.
a secondary field of academic study.
a secret agreement for fraudulent purposes.
a secret code for accessing an account.
a secret code for digital account access.
a secure encrypted connection over the internet.
a security model that requires strict identity verification for every user and device attempting to access resources.
a security system monitoring network traffic.
a selected feature gives the listener an identifiable scene.
a self-contained piece of reusable code.
a self-contained unit of a course.
a senior academic administrator at a university.
a senior teacher at a university.
a sentence fits when both its reference and its role make sense.
a sentence in the passive voice
a sentence is organised around a grammatical head and predicate
a sentence not carried out conditionally.
a sentence with a subject, verb, object, and an adverbial that is essential to the meaning.
a sentence with multiple dependent clauses only
a sentence with one independent clause and at least one dependent clause
a sentence with two independent clauses joined by 'and'
a sentence with two objects: the indirect object (who receives) and the direct object (what is given).
a separate line of code development.
a sequence of automated process steps.
a sequence of drawings outlining film shots.
a sequence of executable program instructions.
a sequence of notes that is musically satisfying.
a sequence of text characters in code.
a series of advertisements for a purpose.
a series of connected processing stages.
a series of performances or events celebrating an art form.
a series of steps for a result.
a serious crime with severe punishment.
a service being open does not alone establish that a particular person can use it at that time.

a service conversation may mention an early collection window, a later shop closing time and a deadline for cancellation. all three can be valid. if asked when the customer must cancel, use the action-specific deadline. a later time for another service does not override it.
a service helping students improve writing.
a service offers online help daily but in-person help only on monday. can a tuesday visitor assume face-to-face assistance?
a set of automated commands for efficiency.
a set of clothes worn together
a set of instructions for a computer.
a set of instructions for cooking a dish.
a set of interacting parts forming a whole.
a set of pages on the internet.
a set of related programs or articles.
a set of rooms for living in
a set of rules or steps used by a computer to solve a problem or complete a task.
a set of three related films or literary works.
a set of topics promoted by media.

a setting introduces the subject, a sequence or explanation develops it, and significance explains why it matters to the speaker. brief notes can represent those relationships without fixing every word. a short part 1 response uses the same relevance principle with less expansion.
a shaped mass of baked bread.
a share falling from 20% to 10% halves; without totals, the amount consumed is unknown.
a share falls from 40% to 30%. give the point fall and relative percentage fall.

a shared digital catalogue several archives created a shared catalogue, but kept the original documents in their own buildings. users could discover material more easily, although access still depended on each archive’s opening hours and handling rules. the catalogue improved discovery rather than creating unrestricted access. future evaluation will examine whether users understand that distinction before travelling.
a shared family does not make the forms interchangeable. sentence structure selects the role; spelling and meaning complete the choice.
a shared growing space makes gardening, cooperation and participation concrete without measuring a social outcome.

a shared map volunteers created a map of public drinking fountains. they initially copied locations from an old council list, but several fountains no longer worked. the group now marks a location as verified only after a recent visit. users can report a fault, although a volunteer checks the report before changing the map. this makes updates slower than an unrestricted system, but it reduces accidental misinformation. the organisers do not promise that every listed fountain will work at the moment of arrival. they advise walkers to carry water on longer journeys and treat the map as useful assistance rather than a guarantee.
a shared meaning can use different sentence patterns
a shared overlap period makes coordination possible.
a shared printer could help pupils.

a shared subject is necessary in these patterns, but not sufficient to express every intended meaning. ‘opening the door, the room became noisy’ does not clearly identify an actor opening the door. use ‘when the staff opened the door, noise entered the room’ if those are the intended actors and events.
a sharp pungent taste opposite of sweet.

a shift notice staff may exchange shifts only after both workers agree and a supervisor approves the change. updating the shared calendar is required after approval, not instead of it. the procedure helps maintain coverage, but an entry in the calendar alone does not make an exchange valid.
a shipping map records inland travel in greater detail than channels.
a shop replaces a warehouse on the same site.
a short checkpoint identifies sampled needs rather than a complete test profile.
a short concluding section at the end of a literary work.
a short individual reflection could show how each student understood the group's decisions, making it easier to identify learning that the shared product may conceal.
a short informal test of understanding.
a short instrumental piece between major sections.
a short introductory piece before a main work.
a short introductory sentence in journalism.
a short menu suits a quick lunch.
a short musical composition inspired by the night.
a short program for automated tasks.
a short reflection can help students explain a decision
a short time expression can change the instruction’s meaning.
a short-term change in growth is not sufficient on its own.
a shortened clause still needs a recoverable actor
a shorter journey from reliable bus service
a shorter lunch menu responds to the service problem.
a show depicting unscripted real life.
a signed letter of authorization from the corporate finance director
a significant difference or separation between groups.
a similar paraphrase can change the required wording.
a simple causal explanation requires a noun head after the two modifiers. explain would leave the noun phrase incomplete.
a simplified representation of a system.
a simplified route for ordinary common nouns when choosing a/an, the or no article. start with what your reader can identify.
a single document on the internet.
a single installment of a series.
a single instruction in programming code.
a single line or stanza in a poem.
a single observed interaction is enough to rank staff permanently.
a single stack containing several books makes number, reference and study-related examples concrete.
a single teaching session or topic.
a single technical note without links
a single unit of academic study.
a situation that makes it possible to do something.
a skill or credential for a profession.
a skill, attribute, or credential that makes someone suitable for a job.
a skilled craftsperson who makes things by hand.
a skillful method for achieving an artistic effect.
a skillful way of doing something.
a skillful way of performing a task.
a slide claiming the whole class was surveyed
a slow sentimental song telling a story of love.
a slow-cooked dish of meat and vegetables.
a small brown fuzzy fruit with green flesh.

a small but common set of nouns change their internal vowel to form the plural. these are all very old english words that have retained their original old english plural pattern (i-mutation). there is no rule for which vowel changes — they must be memorised.

a small change that made my weekends better when did you last learn something with people you had never met? until recently, my answer would have been “years ago”. then i joined a saturday photography walk, and my weekends became much more interesting. the group meets outside the station and chooses a different route each week. you do not need an expensive camera: several members use their phones. what matters is noticing details. one week we photographed reflections; another week we tried to show movement without making every picture completely blurred. the best part is sharing ideas afterwards. nobody pretends to be an expert, so it is easy to ask questions. i have learned useful techniques, but i have also discovered streets i had walked past without noticing. if you want a new activity, i would recommend trying a local group rather than buying more equipment. choose something you are curious about, attend a session, and give yourself permission to be a beginner.
a small crisp root with a peppery taste.

a small design team was building an application to help people find local events. during the first week, its members discussed maps, colour schemes and a long list of possible features. they assumed that users would want as much information as possible. their early design reflected that assumption: each screen contained several panels, filters and buttons. the team was pleased with how much the application could display.
a small dish served before the main course.
a small domed baked bread often containing fruit.
a small edible crustacean with a curved body.
a small electronic device with a specific function.
a small group discussion for advanced study.
a small group sits or lies on a colourful blanket on grass in a park. trees and a path are visible in the background.
a small manufacturer can buy a specialised component abroad but may face disruption if its only shipping route closes.
a small modal substitution can change the requirement. accuracy includes meaning as well as intelligibility.
a small museum redesigned its displays after speaking with visitors. the team wanted clearer information without removing challenging ideas.
a small oily fruit used for oil.
a small part selected to represent a larger group
a small pet that says meow
a small portion of food between meals.
a small red aggregate fruit with tart flavor.
a small round blue berry rich in antioxidants.
a small round red fruit with a single pit.
a small semiconductor component in electronics.
a small software program for mobile devices.
a small sweet baked treat with chocolate chips.
a small sweet orange with easy-to-peel skin.
a small teaching session with a tutor.
a small trial is enough to set a citywide vehicle rule
a smartphone provides a concrete object for discussing changes to familiar services. resistance to a new booking system may have several explanations rather than one fixed cause.
a smartphone provides a concrete object for discussing digital services. separate why someone might choose a service from what reliance on it might later cause.
a smartphone provides a concrete setting for the lesson’s change from paper to a digital service. the reference must connect events, not merely repeat a nearby noun.
a smooth brown nut with a rich buttery taste.
a soft bread roll or a small baked treat.
a software emulation of a physical computer.
a solemn promise to tell the truth.
a solo vocal piece in an opera with orchestral accompaniment.
a solution is relevant when its action addresses a stated problem, cause or consequence.
a solution should act on the identified cause
a solution targets the identified mechanism, subject to practical limits.
a sour liquid used as preservative and flavor.
a sour red berry used in sauces and juices.

a source may explain a promising intervention and then name a limitation. ‘may improve local access’ does not guarantee national success. a dense sentence can hide the qualifier in a subordinate clause, so check modal verbs and restricted populations before accepting a broad answer.
a source of energy that can be used repeatedly and will not run out.
a source of information cited in writing.
a source of information for journalists.
a source of inspiration for a creative artist.
a source says twelve people attended a new session. which is supported: “some people attended” or “the session covered its costs”?
a space for collaborative artistic creation.
a spare session addresses a scheduling risk directly related to the method.

a speaker can discuss the same train service to warn, recommend, complain or explain. the selection of details and the requested response reveal that purpose. gist is a compact account of the whole message, whereas a completion answer may require one precise detail.
a speaker can express approval of the idea itself.
a speaker can favour an idea in principle while withholding commitment until a condition is satisfied.
a speaker says ‘the former shop is now an advice desk.’ which label describes its current use?
a speaker with a strong accent

a speaker’s attitude can be positive, negative or qualified. ‘it was expensive, but i would go again’ accepts a cost yet ends with a favourable recommendation. ‘it was inexpensive, but i would not return’ ends with the opposite judgement. do not score the attitude by counting positive and negative adjectives. work out which statement is being qualified and what the speaker finally endorses.
a speaker’s final position can differ from the position described at the start of an interview.
a special edition of a newspaper.
a specialist in a particular academic field.
a specialized area within an academic major.
a specialized division within a university.
a specific action within a strategy.
a specific area of academic knowledge.

a specific detail makes the answer interpretable rather than merely longer. natural pacing gives the listener time to recover the relationships. a prepared language pattern can support expression, but the selected content still needs to fit the actual interview question.
a specific example connected to the method
a specific function missing in your own argument, such as a causal bridge or a condition. matching paragraph count or replacing ordinary words does not by itself improve reasoning.
a specific request makes the purpose actionable.
a specific section of a contract.
a specific segment of the media market.
a specific subject within a course.
a spice or vegetable from the capsicum plant.
a spiced sauce dish from south asian cuisine.
a spicy pepper used to add heat to dishes.
a spicy root used fresh or dried in cooking.
a spicy tomato-based sauce from mexican cuisine.
a spoken answer develops one relevant response
a spoken or written account of connected events.
a spoken paraphrase retains the speaker’s comparison
a sports day could involve lots of people, although the weather is a risk. could an indoor quiz work instead? which would be easier for us to organise? live interaction still needs a partner.
a sports ticket as a requirement for every visitor
a stack of books gives the library-loan question a concrete object. longer loans may reduce renewal trips while increasing the wait for another reader.
a stage-based preference can distinguish initial feedback from later independent experimentation.
a stall selling newspapers and magazines.
a stand used to hold an artist canvas while painting.
a staple food made from flour and water baked.
a starchy cereal grain eaten as a staple food.
a starchy tuber vegetable used in many dishes.
a statement can be supported, contradicted or left undecided by a passage.
a statement can restrict who is allowed to use a service.
a statement given to news media.
a statement of truth needing evidence.
a statement put forward for argument.
a statement put forward for consideration.

a station displayed predicted crowding levels to help passengers choose quieter trains. some travellers changed departure times, which meant the actual pattern differed from the prediction. the system was not necessarily defective: its information had influenced the behaviour being predicted. evaluators must therefore consider how people respond to a forecast, rather than treating every difference as a simple error.
a station platform gives a concrete setting for a message about access. understanding the practical situation helps distinguish a message’s topic from what it asks people to do.
a station-information setting helps make exact details consequential. the invented sentence below can be grouped for retention, but its words and number must remain intact in a repetition task.
a statistics class adding hours to an already full timetable
a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem.
a storm is imminent; take cover!

a story develops when something changes. for a mistake, identify situation → expectation → mistake → response → result → reflection. for helping someone learn, identify the learner’s difficulty, your demonstration, their attempt and what changed. these sequences give the listener a reason to follow the account.
a story links a turning point to a response
a story or account of connected events
a story or account presented by media.
a story published only by one outlet.
a story recorded as moving images for entertainment.
a story with hidden symbolic meanings beyond the literal.
a stressed word can identify what is being contrasted.
a strong aromatic spice from dried flower buds.
a strong desire to learn or know something.
a strong fabric used as a surface for oil painting.

a strong listener can explain why the tempting detail was wrong for this question. keep the scope modest: a controlled synthetic voice does not demonstrate mastery of every real-world pronunciation. use official samples and varied real listening alongside these lessons when preparing for full delivery conditions.
a strong negative reaction to a political or social development.
a strong vocabulary choice expresses the intended idea naturally and at the appropriate level of specificity.
a stronger quantifier, cause or population needs additional evidence.
a structure improving data retrieval speed.
a structured discussion broadcast on television.
a student can attend the revised date. does a conditional instruction for those who cannot attend automatically apply?
a student doing a first degree
a student gains contacts through a community project

a student magazine asking about a worthwhile activity needs more than a diary entry. the reader wants to understand what happens, why it is enjoyable and whether it might suit them. select details that answer those needs. a title can signal the angle: ‘a small workshop with a useful surprise’ promises an experience, while ‘my article’ supplies no reason to read.
a student magazine wants articles about a worthwhile free-time activity. write a title and opening paragraph that names an activity and gives the reader a reason to continue.
a student pursuing a bachelor's degree.
a student studying beyond a bachelor's degree.
a student studying beyond a first degree
a student website wants reviews of a place suitable for studying. describe its facilities, evaluate strengths and limitations, and recommend it to a particular reader. write 140–190 words.
a student who leaves school prematurely.

a study can be reliable in the sense that its procedure produces consistent measurements, yet fail to measure the concept the researcher intended. a timed typing task might give stable results but provide a narrow picture of writing ability. repetition and relevance are therefore separate considerations when evaluating evidence.
a study finds students who exercise also report less stress. name one reason causation remains uncertain.
a study group complete the eight gaps using one word each. read the connected account before answering.

a study investigates a question using a method. a sample is the set of cases or participants examined. an outcome is what is measured or observed. these language concepts support reading; the fictional examples are not scientific or medical advice.
a study judgement depends on the evidence collected
a study judgement is bounded by its evidence
a style of cooking associated with a particular culture.
a subgroup and a time restriction both carry meaning
a subject and a tensed verb follow although.

a subject question is different: ‘who teaches the course?’ already asks for the subject and does not normally add do. identify what information is missing before rearranging pieces; not every question uses the same order.
a subordinate clause expresses a logical relationship

a subordinate clause normally depends on another clause to complete the message. although introduces concession; because introduces a reason. however connects ideas as an adverb and does not join two independent clauses in the same grammatical way as a conjunction.
a subsidy could keep a late service affordable. shift workers would then have a way home after ordinary routes stop, though low passenger numbers might make each journey expensive to support.
a subtle difference in meaning expression or color.
a successful completion of a goal.

a successful email does more than mention a topic. the recipient should understand what happened and what response is needed. separate the task’s required actions, then give each enough detail to be useful. a scheduling problem needs the unavailable time and a proposed alternative, not a lengthy apology with no next step. asking whether material is needed is different from claiming it has already been requested. adjust directness to the relationship, while keeping the message concise and clear. the linked choices inspect coverage and communication; these choices do not evaluate a complete email or assign a toefl writing score.
a sudden major advance in technology.

a suffix can signal a noun, adjective or other form, but the sentence determines which meaning and form are possible. singular or plural reference and positive or negative meaning may also matter. in the exam task, any supplied letters constrain the completion as well as the context.
a suggestion as the best course.
a suit is required for formal occasions.
a suitable option satisfies the complete requirement, including its restrictions.
a summary of the main trends in a chart or graph
a supply chain connects production to transport
a supply chain connects stages of production and distribution, so a change at one stage can affect participants elsewhere.
