activate an earlier skill: identify the complete claim in “shops should stop giving away bags because repeated use reduces waste.” shops should stop giving away bags is the position. the because-clause supplies a reason. a statement such as “shopping bags are common” names the topic but does not decide the question.

active past: ‘staff inspected the room.’ passive past: ‘the room was inspected.’ active future: ‘staff will inspect the room.’ passive future: ‘the room will be inspected.’ present perfect: ‘the room has been inspected.’ the auxiliary chain carries time and aspect; inspected remains the participle.
active support for a legal cause.
active voice identifies what provides the explanation.
active voice keeps the agent clear.
active: shakespeare wrote hamlet. → passive: hamlet was written by shakespeare.
active: she gave me a gift.
active: someone stole my wallet. → passive: my wallet was stolen.
active: the chef cooked the meal. → passive: the meal was cooked by the chef.
active: they offered him the job.

active: “staff checked the equipment on monday.” passive: “the equipment was checked on monday.” both describe the completed check. “students who have completed induction may use the room” limits access to a defined group; it does not say training is optional.

active: “the team repairs the door.” passive: “the door is repaired.” for a completed past account, change only the auxiliary to was. for a future arrangement, use will be. complete “the door ___ ___ repaired already” in a present-perfect account before adding any agent.
activity of buying and selling on large scale.
activity of starting and managing new businesses.

actor clause: “workers remove stones.” affected subject: stones. be agrees with the plural subject, so “stones are removed.” complete “the clay ___ (shape) into pots.” shaped is the participle; clay is singular in this material sense.
actors, actions and explanations form an intelligible line of thought.
actual use supports a demand claim; it does not establish reduced sick leave.
actually = in fact (not 'now'). currently = at this time.
actually, i am working now. (meaning currently)
actually, i don't agree with you.
actually, i'd like to offer my time. i'm interested in volunteering.
actually, no. we've been waiting for over forty minutes for our main course.
actually, sorry or instead can replace a specific earlier detail.
actually, the meeting is at 3 pm, not 2 pm.
adapt requests, explanations and closings to formal, semi-formal and informal relationships.
adapt to a formal information request
adapting a cooling idea to structural limits

adapting a workshop covers the problem and response across the paragraph. a bicycle wheel is merely a local topic. the paragraph is invented; the photograph provides context rather than evidence about this particular workshop’s queues or history.
adapting smoothly to different screen sizes.
adaptive testing means correct answers may lead to more challenging subsequent questions.
adaptive testing technology adjusts question difficulty based on your performance. correct answers lead to harder questions.
add a complete line of reasoning

add a concrete difficulty and its resolution to the workshop plan. check one possible sequence: the brake rubbed against the wheel; the neighbour demonstrated centring it; later the learner adjusted it independently.
add a contribution that develops a shared question
add a genuine condition in a different context

add a possible limitation to the model without abandoning its main point. check: unexpected work can disrupt a timetable, so the speaker leaves a spare study session. explain how that detail remains related to organisation.
add a qualification to an earlier general claim.
add a related point after a complete sentence.

add a response for someone who has internet but struggles to navigate the form. check one plausible measure: a clearly labelled assisted-booking service or an accessible form. explain why providing internet alone might not solve that particular barrier.
add an -ing activity after a prepositional expression.

add an example of a changed decision. check: a group might replace a broad survey with focused interviews after finding its first questions unclear. explain what a reflection on that change could reveal.
add an original mechanism or application to a discussion.
add diced aubergine/eggplant to the curry.
add duration only after the basic relationship is secure
add not after an auxiliary; otherwise use do/does/did not + base verb. standard english normally avoids a second negative for the same meaning.

add one sentence explaining a risk of an entirely unrestricted elective choice. check one possible extension: prerequisites may make some modules unsuitable for beginners, so advisers should identify accessible options.
add structure only when it expresses a relationship
adding a noun phrase or an -ing activity
adding a point that reinforces the argument.
adding a prefix to a word
adding access may take several working days
adding an additional reason, often a stronger one.
adding an important point, often stronger than the previous one.
adding comparison prompts as the whole exhibition strategy
adding detail to make a point more exact.
adding homes near transport with infrastructure planning
adding new information to a sentence
adding solar estimates made it impossible to construct any comparison.
adding the singular verb ending repairs agreement. it supplies no new date, guarantee or claim that every visitor will make a booking.
additional cost of producing one more unit.
additional effect of one more unit of activity.
additional material at the end of a document.
additional process evidence can help evaluate a claim rather than relying on the reflection alone.
address a concern is a natural collocation.
address all three criteria in every response. record yourself and self-evaluate.
address every requested action in an email
address every requested action in an email. match tone to the recipient. propose a specific and feasible next step.
address the reader directly: 'you should visit', 'you will love'
addresses all parts of the prompt, presents a well-developed position throughout, and provides extended supporting arguments.
adds a stronger, more precise, or more emphatic statement.
adds an additional, often stronger, reason or argument.
adds another important reinforcing point, formal.
adherence to rules regulations and standards.
adjective + noun in english (a good teacher), not noun + adjective.
adjectives come before nouns: a red car (not: a car red)
adjectives come before the noun in english, not after as in arabic.
adjectives come before the noun in english, not after. arabic places adjectives after the noun, causing this common error.
adjectives: a sharp rise, a significant increase, a gradual decline, a slight drop, a steady growth.
adjust tone without losing the request
adjusted for inflation to reflect true value.
adjusting lighting to balance access and ecology
adjusting to actual climate change effects.
adjustment to environmental conditions over generations.
admiration for someone's qualities abilities or achievements.
admittedly concedes a point that qualifies the broader argument.
admittedly the weather was bad, but the vacation was still nice.
admittedly, the initial cost is high. however, the long-term savings are significant.
adoption of cultural traits of another group.
adult b2 first: one compulsory essay plus one task selected from three; write 140–190 words per response.
advanced academic distinction for high grades.
advanced grammar mastery: negative inversion, cleft sentences, participle clauses
advanced stage of human social development.
advancement to a higher position or rank.
advantages-disadvantages: do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages? state clearly which side is more significant.

adverbs can also be compared. short adverbs (one syllable) add '-er' and '-est'. longer adverbs use 'more' and 'most'. some adverbs have irregular forms like 'well → better → best' and 'badly → worse → worst'.
adverbs of degree ('very much') come after the object, not before it.
adverbs of degree (very much, really) come after the object, not before it. arabic sentence structure allows v + adv + o, but english requires v + o + adv.
adverbs of frequency (always, never, often) come after the verb 'to be' but before other main verbs. arabic places them differently.
adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) → before main verb: she always arrives on time.
adverbs of manner (quickly, carefully) → after verb: he drove carefully.
adverbs: rose sharply, increased significantly, declined gradually, dropped slightly, grew steadily.
advice = noun (it has 'ice' like 'rice', a thing). advise = verb (it has 'ise' like 'rise', an action).
advice and information are normally uncountable in this use. pieces supplies a countable unit for advice; the tutors' number does not make advice itself plural.
advice desk. former and now distinguish the historical use from the present one; both nouns may be heard, but they do not describe the same time.
advise + person + to: he advised us to study.
affect = verb (action). effect = noun (result). 'the medicine affected me. the effect was positive.'
after 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive. it takes a gerund (-ing form).
after 'used to', the verb is in the base form (infinitive without 'to'), not the past tense.
after 'used to', use the base form (infinitive) of the verb: 'used to wake', not 'used to woke'.

after a corrected repetition, use a different sentence heard once rather than reciting the same text again. in the live seven-item set, compare omission, substitution and order for each prompt, then listen for intelligibility. do not add an opinion or reason to an exact repetition.

after a delay, reconstruct the three frames from their intended meanings. the checked reading tasks demonstrate contextual interpretation; choosing and using the expression yourself is a further production step.
after a later writing task, replace one inflated or overly strong expression with precise ordinary language and explain the meaning change. do not replace a correct word simply because it is short.

after a live choice, explain the nearest wrong option in one sentence: wrong actor, changed outcome, widened scope or strengthened certainty. if the evidence is found but the answer is still uncertain, return to the exact clause; another whole-text scan does not resolve a may/must distinction.

after a modal, use a base verb: ‘the procedure can reduce delays.’ after an article and adjective, find the noun head: ‘a clear description’. describe is a verb and descriptive an adjective, so neither completes that noun phrase alone.
after a preposition in formal english: 'the person to whom...'

after a preposition, an action often uses -ing: before leaving, after checking, look forward to meeting. in look forward to, to is a preposition, not the infinitive marker. complete “we look forward to ___ from you (hear).”

after a recorded response, compare the transcript for missing words, substitutions and changed order. then listen to the actual recording for whether important words and endings are understandable. a written transcript can show grammatical accuracy but cannot establish how clearly it was spoken.
after a wrong live answer, name the decision that failed: countability, sound or identifiability. repeating “second mention means the” will not repair a first-mention shared-knowledge error.

after a wrong match, write expectation → final evaluation and quote the contrast that connects them. if the speaker stays mixed, keep both parts: useful content / unsuitable pace. an option saying entirely useless is too strong when the source praises useful content. an option saying completely satisfied drops the pace concern.

after an error, replay the relevant turn and identify the information role before reading the transcript. once the meaning is clear, replay without text to check recognition. after another listening module, explain a new speaker’s initial motive and current judgement without copying full sentences.

after an introductory participle clause, inspect the main subject immediately. ask whether that subject can perform or undergo the participle event. incorrect: ‘having inspected the building, several faults were found.’ improved: ‘having inspected the building, the engineer found several faults.’ or retain a full passive account: ‘after the building was inspected, several faults were found.’
after an opener such as could you tell me, use statement order inside the embedded question.
after another listening module, retrieve a different time or amount in a new sentence. do not claim accent comprehension from repeatedly recognising one familiar recording.

after another module, choose a fresh follow-up for the one weakness documented in your plan. use official sample delivery for full-format rehearsal where needed, and retain local results as local evidence. xp, a word total or a small fixed quiz does not establish the current official score.

after another module, compare original and fresh responses for that single target. keep missing evidence marked unassessed and seek qualified review for persistent writing or speech problems. retained xp and local accuracy remain participation and task evidence, not official score conversions.
after another module, produce a new sentence using reliable or reliability and explain its frame. a relevant technical word helps when its role and evidence are clear.

after another reading task, write a yes claim, a no claim and a genuinely unanswerable claim about a fresh paragraph. check that a no claim has incompatible evidence, rather than just stronger wording. decide each label from evidence rather than an expected answer sequence.

after another speaking module, choose a different everyday turning point and tell it without the supplied frame. use the retained model audio for comparison after your attempt; written notes alone cannot demonstrate fluency.
after another vocabulary lesson, retrieve a whole phrase from a real communication need. a natural collocation does not make an unsupported conclusion true.
after another writing task, retrieve a noun and verb version of a new comparison. check whether each claim describes recorded endpoints or invents the curve between them.
after being washed, the fruit is crushed and pressed, and the resulting liquid is bottled.

after checking, classify the error before replaying. if the transcript was understood immediately, practise recognition of the exact sound group. if the supplied-versus-required relationship was misunderstood even in writing, paraphrase it first: organisers supply brushes; participant supplies apron. fresh audio, not a reread transcript alone, tests whether the distinction has transferred.

after checking, explain one mentioned distractor’s true status. replay the acceptance or condition clause and test the distinction on new audio later. the task determines whether a practical consequence or final arrangement is being asked for.

after checking, identify the exact missed relationship. if you wrote a consequence under cause, rewrite it as an arrow. if you selected precipitation for evaporation, study the contextual meaning and listen to the word again. do not solve a semantic confusion by merely playing the whole lecture faster.

after checking, record whether the error came from finding the wrong passage, misunderstanding a word, losing a qualifier or running out of time. practise the weak step on an unfamiliar source. faster rereading of the same answers can reflect memory rather than improved reading.

after checking, replay the clause that attaches the answer to its category. if the transcript was clear but the sound was missed, rehearse that short group and replay without text. if the wrong customer was selected, repair the category record first. return to that distinction in a new recording after another module.

after checking, select one difficult phrase. listen while reading once, then listen without text and state the arrangement. finally use a new recording with the same kind of detail but different facts. merely recognising a memorised transcript cannot establish unfamiliar listening comprehension.

after checking, write a short ownership note: writer / quoted stakeholder / factual report. then compare the complete meaning of the chosen answer with the source clause. this is useful for general training’s longer text and for evaluative language inside practical notices.
after completing the training, students can reserve the room independently.
after each test, spend at least as much time reviewing as taking it.

after feedback, attach each incorrect time or action to the verb it actually belongs to. replay that clause without reading. later, retrieve the difference between a conditional instruction and an instruction applying to everyone on fresh audio.

after feedback, explain the closest distractor’s conversational mismatch: wrong information, unperformed action or unsupported certainty. revisit one distinction on a new spoken question later. a transcript can clarify the speech act; recognition still needs the audio.

after feedback, label each decisive link: reference, time, contrast, cause or vocabulary chain. write a short explanation such as ‘the new venue needs an earlier move’ rather than ‘it sounds right’. then practise a new gap that uses the same relationship with different nouns. that tests whether you learned cohesion rather than the old sentence order.

after feedback, quote the phrase establishing the stance, then state what cannot be concluded. for a sound-recognition error, replay the phrase; for an inference error, explain why the stronger or weaker alternative goes beyond it. try a fresh qualified judgement before declaring the skill secure.

after feedback, record orientation, status or hierarchy as the error cause. revisit different audio with the same demand later. this mixed lesson checkpoint is not a full forty-question ielts listening test.

after feedback, record the action and its governing clause. if two conditions seem to conflict, check whether they apply to different groups, times or stages. do not import a rule from your own workplace to resolve a reading question. the supplied text is the evidence.

after feedback, record the word’s contextual meaning, grammar and one natural partner: conduct a study, collect evidence, analyse data, acknowledge a limitation. then retrieve it in a fresh sentence rather than copying a glossary definition alone.

after feedback, separate a grammar repair from a numerical or causal repair. on a later day, write a new from/to/by comparison without a frame and explain what information would be needed to claim cause or total spending.

after feedback, trace a reference expression and define one unfamiliar term from its local explanation. return later to an unfamiliar paragraph and reject the closest strengthened summary in your own words.
after finishing dinner, we went to the door
after he finished work, he went for a walk.
after he finished work, he went home.
after i had brushed my teeth, i went to bed.
after negative adverbials (never, rarely, seldom), invert subject and auxiliary: 'never have i...'
after nine and before nine establish opposite sides of the boundary.

after reconstructing an inversion, rewrite it in ordinary order to verify the event and time. if you cannot explain the focus difference, use the simpler version in independent writing until control improves. no quota of inversions or clefts establishes an examination band.

after recording, point to the clause that answers the demand and the example that supports its reason. if the example becomes a long unrelated story, shorten it. later, answer a new why-question with one clear mechanism before adding a qualification.

after review, replay the phrase that connects cause and effect, then listen without the transcript. in the new stream and packaging recordings, choose your own note labels. later, reconstruct one mechanism from a fresh short explanation, retaining its implementation limit.

after review, underline one place where you explain how rather than simply say useful. if it is absent, repair that paragraph. on your next writing day, close this chapter and build a new paragraph from a claim of your own: one explanation, one relevant illustration and a limit only where it contributes. revisit the sentence step if meaning is lost in the grammar.
after reviewing the evidence, the committee changed its advice.

after revising, choose unfamiliar material with the same demand. a new letter should change recipient or purpose; a new listening extract should change its facts; a fresh speaking response should develop another event. success then provides better evidence of a learned method than repeating an old answer key.

after submitting, explain the closest wrong option using the clause it changes; do not merely record its letter. in the next reading module, retrieve the difference between a topic and a controlling idea, then write one purpose question about its new text. if a new passage has a different structure, map that structure rather than forcing every source into a trial template.
after that time or after that event. indicates sequence in formal writing.
after that time, it expanded rapidly across europe.
after that time. used to indicate what happened next in sequence.
after the cycling group rejected the plan, the council consulted its representatives.

after the final set, choose two taught expressions and make new sentences without a key-word prompt: one with a pronoun and one with a different tense. return after another module and explain which form is separable. the checked tasks reuse taught language in fresh frames; independent expression selection needs this additional sentence-production step.

after the full article, ask a reader to name what participants do and who would enjoy it. if they cannot, revise the sentence where you replaced description with vague praise. on a later day, write a new opening about a different place without the i-had-never frame.

after the interview, it is a good idea to send a thank-you email to the interviewer. this shows your appreciation and reminds them of your interest in the job. if you do not hear back within a week or two, you can follow up politely to ask about the status of your application.

after the live paragraphs, label one sentence’s function and identify its exact referent. if the label is “new unrelated topic”, reorganise before replacing vocabulary. revisit a different paragraph after the next writing module and repeat the test without the role prompts.

after the live task, underline every finite verb and label its evidence role. revisit after another grammar lesson with different dates. if the grammar is correct but a proposal becomes a fact, revise the status word as well as the tense.

after the mixed sources, explain one summary option’s lost qualification and one practical answer’s condition. create a new question about another paragraph and identify whether it asks for detail, judgement or procedure.

after the mixed token set, write a new sentence with one corrected pattern and explain its complement. return after another module and choose a different verb from the same group. the exact token order checks a bounded construction; fresh sentence production checks whether you can use it without the supplied pieces.

after the museum task, write one new sentence with an adjective and another with its related adverb, without looking at a base-word prompt. revisit them after the next module and explain the jobs. producing a form from a supplied root demonstrates a narrower skill than choosing the expression yourself.

after the new live mixed-question sources, explain the closest wrong option rather than recording its letter alone. revisit an unfamiliar paragraph later and retrieve which procedure fits its question. this is a short mixed-skills checkpoint, not a complete calibrated ielts reading test.

after the new live summary, label a wrong answer as source selection, transferred grammar, word limit or strengthened meaning. retrieve the same distinction on a fresh paragraph after the next reading lesson.

after the new pie-chart and table tasks, underline each comparison’s population and unit. revisit one calculation after the next writing module without looking at its answer. if the result is correct but the sentence says people instead of share, revise the meaning as well as the arithmetic.
after the next grammar module, retrieve an unless example and explain its exception in plain english. a correct remembered sentence is only the starting point for a fresh scenario.

after the next listening lesson, retrieve one missed relationship in fresh audio. use transcripts for diagnosis after an attempt; a written explanation alone cannot demonstrate recognition of the new recording.

after the next module, return without looking at your answers and explain why “did not went”, “has wrote” and “were check” need repair. use new subjects and events. a correct answer copied from the chapter does not establish that you can choose a viewpoint in fresh context. the existing exhibition, research-visit and residence/investment tasks provide that next application.

after the next reading session, retrieve one reference link and one qualifier from an unfamiliar paragraph. diagnose a slow search separately from an unsupported inference; faster recognition of a memorised answer does not establish improved comprehension.
after the next speaking lesson, tell a different learning event without the supplied frame. a written plan can show organisation; actual speech is required to judge continuity and intelligibility.

after the next speaking module, answer a new familiar-topic question with no written sentence frame. listen for the particular repair you practised here, such as a missing reason-clause subject or unclear phrase boundary. b2 interview rehearsal is solo evidence; real paired interaction needs another person, and the checklist does not automatically assess pronunciation or proficiency.

after the next study session, retrieve one weak sentence from each response and repair its task-specific problem before surface language. this mixed checkpoint covers two writing families; build a sentence still requires separate practice.

after the next writing module, rewrite one informal request for an unfamiliar organiser. keep the factual need but change greeting, request and closing consistently. check whether the reader can act on it; changing only hi to dear does not complete the register change.

after the targeted heading task, write one gist question and one detail question about a new paragraph. answer each with the appropriate amount of evidence. on a later day, retrieve why a memorable example can be a correct detail answer but an incomplete heading.
after the timer ends, read what you wrote and underline 3 things to improve.

after the volunteer assessment, invent a new requirement that would change the correct match. name the exact failed condition, then check all profiles again. this tests comprehension of the source rather than remembering an a/b/c/d order.

after the volunteer-training assessment, choose one paragraph whose example fails to explain its claim and revise that connection. later, reconstruct the decision principle of a different essay without copying the model’s phrases.

after the workshop assessment, choose a corrected gap and explain both anchors without quoting its whole sentence. later, write a fresh three-sentence sequence with a demonstrative reference such as this change. remove the middle sentence and check whether a reader can tell what information is missing.

after training, your supervisor must confirm which procedures your project requires. access will then be added to your account. this sequence may take several working days, so plan experiments accordingly. it is intended to support safe, appropriate use, not to certify expertise in every possible imaging method.
after two, visitors need an appointment.
after which or as a result of which. indicates that something immediately followed.
after winning the competition, i was on cloud nine for days.
agent obvious: he was arrested. (by the police — obvious)
agent unimportant: the meeting has been postponed. (who postponed it doesn't matter)
agent unknown: my phone was stolen. (i don't know who)
agent who arranges transactions between parties.
agree is the finite verb here; no extra be form is needed.
agreeable friendly and enjoyable interpersonal manner.
agreement connects the subject head to its verb
agreement is a noun; agree is a verb.
agreement needs support, contradiction needs incompatible evidence, and missing information needs an identified gap.
agreement that allows someone to do something
agreement to exchange cash flows between two parties.
agreement with the writer depends on whose claim the question asks about.
ah yes, mr. hassan. a double room for three nights. is that correct?

ai has many benefits. it can process information much faster than humans and work 24 hours a day without getting tired. in healthcare, ai is used to help doctors diagnose diseases more accurately. in business, ai automates repetitive tasks and improves efficiency.

ai is already part of our daily lives in many ways. when you use a smartphone, ai helps with voice assistants like siri and google assistant. streaming services like netflix use ai to recommend movies and shows, and email services use ai to filter spam messages.

ai works by using large amounts of data and special algorithms called machine learning. these algorithms learn patterns from data and improve over time without being explicitly programmed for every task. the more data an ai system receives, the better it becomes at its job.
aim for 100-150 words. proofread quickly for major errors.
aim for frequent error-free sentences with a range of complex structures.
aim for no more than 90 seconds per question on average. some take 30-60 seconds, others up to 2 minutes.
air pollution is a major problem.
all eligible voters in a particular area.
all employees working in an organization.
all of whom refers to people in the preceding group. of is already supplied, and the relative phrase needs whom rather than a new independent they clause.
all plans: british council free practice tests, ielts liz youtube, idp ielts app, bbc 6 minute english.
all property owned by a deceased person.
all residents stopped driving because buses were free.
all the words that you know in a language.
all things considered, it seems clear that ...
all things considered. formed from 'every' + 'thing'. refers to all possible items or aspects.
all things you need for the trip are packed in this suitcase.
all things; each thing. formed from 'every' + 'thing'. refers to all items or aspects.
alliteration is the repetition of initial consonant sounds (e.g., 'peter piper picked').
allocate drafting and checking effort according to actual demands.
allocation of money expecting future profit.

allow takes an object plus a to-infinitive in this pattern: “the pass allows visitors to enter.” partly complete “the timetable allows staff ___ leave earlier.” let instead normally uses object plus base verb: “let staff leave.” do not transfer one pattern mechanically to the other.
allowing light to pass through clearly.
allowing students to learn at their own speed without strict deadlines.
allows does not mean guarantees a booking for every visitor.
along the same lines, we should also consider the environmental benefits.
already, ever, never, yet → present perfect.
alright, let's vote on doing a trial run. all in favor?
alternating between two or more languages in conversation
alternating crop types to preserve soil.
although + clause: most common, neutral: although it was hard, i did it.
although already introduces the subordinate contrast clause. in this standard structure, an extra but is unnecessary. alternatively, remove although and connect two main clauses with but.
although classes exist, but adults work
although evening classes widen access, childcare can still be a barrier
although introduces a clause; despite introduces a noun phrase or an -ing form. both can express an unexpected contrast.
although introduces a fact that makes the outcome unexpected.
although introduces concession; because introduces a reason.
although it is shorter, it is slower.
although it rained, we went for a walk.
although it was hard, i finished it.
although it was raining, we decided to go ahead with the outdoor event.

although marks a concession between rain and continuing to walk. because gives rain as the reason for using umbrellas. both constructions contain clauses, but they organise the meaning differently; an elaborate sentence is useful only when the relationship stays clear.
although marks a concession: shorter might suggest faster, yet the route is slower. because instead states why it is slower. changing the connector changes the relationship.
although online study is convenient, but it offers less personal contact.
although online study is convenient, it offers less personal contact.
although the main gallery is closed, the exhibition on the upper floor remains open.
although the pilot was small, its findings justify a larger trial.
although the results were encouraging, the researchers recommended a longer trial.
although the road was icy, the bus arrived. → despite the icy road, the bus arrived.
although the room is small, it has everything we need.
although the room is small, it meets our needs.
although the route is shorter, the climb makes it slower.
although the scheme costs more, it reaches remote villages. a full argument should then explain how much that wider access matters relative to cost.
although the scheme is costly, it may improve access. the reverse ordering is also possible if the intended emphasis changes.
although the survey was small, it revealed a concern worth investigating.
although the task was difficult, she solved it.
although the trial found greater satisfaction, it did not measure long-term outcomes. the sentence accepts the finding while limiting what the study establishes; it does not deny the finding.

although the trial involved only a small group, participants reported that the new service was easier to use. that finding is useful because it identifies a possible improvement in access. it does not establish a lasting benefit, since the evaluation ended after one month. a longer trial should examine whether the initial satisfaction continues and whether users can complete their tasks without additional help. the limitation narrows the conclusion rather than making the entire exercise worthless.
although the trial was short, it revealed a problem that deserves further study.
although the trial was short, it was useful.
although the trial was small, its findings justified further investigation.
although/even though + subject + verb | despite/in spite of + noun/gerund
always acknowledge the counter-argument before refuting it
always behaving in the same way.
always leave 30-60 seconds for proofreading at the end of each task.
always present simple in both clauses.
always prioritize materials updated for 2026 format to reflect new question types.
always use 'the' before both comparatives: the more... the more... (not: more... more...)
always write an overview paragraph summarising the big picture (not individual data points).
always: depend on, not depend from.
am → i: i am invited to the party.
among these volunteers does not mean among everyone.
among — three or more items, not distinct
amount added to cost price to determine selling price.
amount by which expenses exceed revenue earned.
amount of goods money can buy over time.
amount of matter contained in an object.
amount of money needed to sustain basic lifestyle.
amount of money required to produce something.
amount of product obtained from reaction.
amount owed by a business to its creditors.
amount paid for an insurance policy.
amount paid out of pocket before insurance applies.
amount remaining after all deductions are made.
amounts owed to a business by its customers.

an -ing clause can give overlapping activity or a reason: ‘checking the figures, the researcher noticed a discrepancy.’ having + past participle marks an earlier completed action: ‘having checked the figures, the researcher revised the report.’ the main clause supplies the narrative time; having checked establishes sequence relative to it.
an -ing form often expresses an active relationship; a past participle often expresses a passive one.

an -ing form often expresses an active relationship; a past participle often expresses a passive one. having + past participle can mark an earlier completed action. the shortened clause does not independently establish tense, and its actor must make sense in the full sentence.
an abandoned option can be heard accurately but given the wrong status.
an abstract explanation becomes clear through a mechanism
an abstract explanation connects judgement to mechanism
an abstract idea or general notion.
an academic award conferred by a university.

an academic discussion contribution should make a clear, relevant point and develop it. formality means suitability to the setting, not using the longest possible synonym. simple words such as help, people and problem are not automatically wrong. a contraction is not an automatic failure; judge tone and clarity within the whole response. address a classmate’s reasoning when it helps your own argument, and add an explanation or concrete application. you can acknowledge a concern without abandoning your position. the current task is a short developed contribution to the specific classroom discussion.
an academic discussion is clear when its claims, reasons and qualifications are expressed accurately for the audience.
an academic discussion response connects a position to the professor’s question and develops a contribution to the exchange.
an academic publication for research articles.
an academic seminar for research discussion.
an academic talk can report a relationship while treating its explanation as uncertain or incomplete.
an academic talk on urban streams
an accessible copy would allow registration.
an accessible entrance could be created on the east side.
an accurate familiar verb is more useful than an impressive-sounding overstatement. match the strength of the word to the support available.
an accurately repeated sentence supplies evidence about that attempt.
an act breaking a law or rule.
an active clause presents the actor as subject; a passive clause can present the affected entity as subject.

apex global technologies — remote workstation health and ergonomics protocol section a: workstation self-assessment under the display screen equipment (dse) regulations, all hybrid staff who conduct computer-based work from home for more than two days per working week are mandated to complete a digital ergonomic self-assessment within thirty calendar days of onboarding. employees must ensure that their display screen is positioned directly at eye level, roughly an arm's length (50–70 cm) away from the face, to avoid cervical spinal strain. section b: company equipment stipend the organization provides a one-off non-taxable equipment stipend of up to £400 to procure an approved ergonomic task chair, an external monitor, and a height-adjustable laptop riser. in order to claim reimbursement through the hr expense portal, employees must submit itemized receipts accompanied by photographic confirmation that the equipment has been assembled and configured in compliance with safety standards. section c: working hours and screen breaks to mitigate visual fatigue and musculoskeletal strain, staff should adhere to the '20-20-20 rule': every twenty minutes of sustained screen use, gaze at an object situated at least twenty feet away for a minimum of twenty seconds. in addition, line managers must ensure that employees schedule at least five to ten minutes of non-screen administrative tasks or physical mobility breaks for every continuous hour of keyboard input. section d: incident and injury reporting in the event that an employee experiences persistent discomfort, repetitive strain symptoms, or sustains a physical injury while performing professional duties in their home workspace, they must notify their line manager and lodge an official incident report via the apex health portal within forty-eight hours. failure to report in a timely manner may invalidate statutory workers' compensation claims.

complete original model contribution; not an official scored response: i would support one elective if students can choose from a manageable list and receive advice about workload. mina is right that exploring another field can reveal interests, but the benefit is greater when students can connect it with their main studies. for example, a biology student taking an introductory statistics class could learn tools for interpreting later laboratory results. leo's concern about time is also reasonable, so the elective should replace another optional requirement rather than simply add hours to an already full timetable. this would preserve a serious opportunity to explore while limiting unnecessary pressure. the aim should be a useful connection between subjects, not collecting unrelated credits merely to satisfy a rule.

complete original model essay: universities often encourage students to work with local organisations. whether this activity should be compulsory is more controversial. although a required project could introduce many students to valuable experiences, i believe participation should normally remain voluntary, with universities making it easier for students to take part. supporters of compulsory projects argue that education should develop social responsibility as well as subject knowledge. some students may never consider volunteering until it appears in their timetable. working with a neighbourhood group can show them how their skills help others. for example, engineering students who improve access to a community building can apply classroom knowledge to a practical problem. a requirement may also distribute these opportunities more evenly instead of limiting them to students who already have useful contacts. however, a universal obligation can create difficulties for students with demanding circumstances. someone who works evenings to pay rent or cares for a relative may struggle to attend a fixed project session. if participation becomes another condition for graduating, the policy could penalise these students even when they contribute to their communities in other ways. requiring attendance also does not guarantee thoughtful engagement; some participants may focus only on completing their hours. a more effective approach would combine strong encouragement with flexible opportunities. universities could offer short projects, remote tasks and optional academic credit. advisers could help students choose work connected to their interests while recognising responsibilities outside campus. this would preserve meaningful choice without treating community activity as unimportant. in conclusion, compulsory service has a reasonable educational purpose, but its costs are unevenly distributed. accessible voluntary projects are more likely to produce engaged participation while respecting students' different situations.

demographic shifts toward an older populace have sparked intense political and economic debate across advanced industrialized economies. while critics contend that a graying demographic imposes an unsustainable fiscal burden on healthcare systems and pension funds, proponents argue that senior citizens provide invaluable social capital and economic stability. in this essay, i will examine both perspectives before arguing that while the challenges are undeniable, proactive governance can harness the substantial benefits of an experienced senior cohort. on the one hand, the fiscal apprehensions associated with demographic aging are legitimate. an escalating dependency ratio—where fewer active workers contribute income taxes to support a burgeoning retired populace—strains state welfare coffers. furthermore, chronic age-related comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease and cognitive impairment necessitate intensive, long-term medical care, driving up public healthcare expenditures. in nations like japan and italy, this dynamic has threatened to compromise municipal budgets and decelerate overall economic productivity. on the other hand, portraying older generations exclusively as economic liabilities is a reductionist fallacy. senior citizens contribute immensely to the social fabric through unpaid domestic labor, particularly childcare, which enables younger parents to remain in the active workforce. moreover, many experienced professionals choose to delay retirement or transition into mentorship roles, transferring tacit institutional knowledge to emerging leaders. additionally, affluent seniors drive the expanding 'silver economy' in sectors such as tourism, wellness, and cultural enterprises. in conclusion, although the demographic transition toward an older society undoubtedly necessitates substantial fiscal reforms—such as gradually increasing the statutory retirement age and modernizing preventative healthcare—it does not represent an economic dead end. with forward-thinking social policies, aging populations can enrich communities both culturally and economically.

demonstration mechanism: experience helps identify problems a beginner may overlook. illustration: a guide can explain why a route takes longer in wet conditions. limit: an old recommendation may not include a new closure.

demonstration: “a lifeguard explained the lane rules before i entered. that made the first visit less confusing because i knew where a slow swimmer should go.” the visit supplies the evidence; the because-clause explains its value. it is more informative than “the staff are amazing.”

demonstration: “does the timetable include a break?” does already carries the singular present marking; include stays base. complete “do the sessions ___ (include) a break?” and repair “the timetable can changes.” do not add -s after every singular subject without checking the auxiliary.

demonstration: “extra laptops could help visitors without a device. however, they would still need a time when they can reach the library. could we compare that with opening later on saturday?” the turn acknowledges, qualifies and invites comparison. it does not require a memorised phrase if the relationship stays clear.

demonstration: “giving away fewer disposable bags could reduce waste. customers who reuse one sturdy bag need fewer new bags on later visits. for example, keeping a folded bag in a work bag makes reuse practical during routine shopping.” sentence one makes the claim; sentence two explains how; sentence three makes the mechanism observable. “it is good and beneficial” would merely repeat the evaluation.

demonstration: “i like choosing the ingredients.” subject i and finite verb like make the answer complete. add a reason: “i can adapt a meal to what my family enjoys.” join when ready: “i like choosing the ingredients because i can adapt a meal to what my family enjoys.” avoid “i am like cooking because is useful”: like is already the finite verb, and the reason clause needs a subject.

english distinguishes between countable and uncountable nouns in comparisons. 'more' is used with all nouns. 'fewer' is used with countable nouns (books, people, chairs). 'less' is used with uncountable nouns (water, money, time). this is an important distinction for arabic speakers.
english does not allow double negatives. use 'anything' with a negative verb, or 'nothing' with a positive verb.

english does not have a distinct dative case form. instead, the indirect object is shown through word order (i gave him a book = him is indirect, book is direct) or with the preposition 'to' or 'for' (i gave a book to him). the indirect object receives the direct object.
english does not use double negatives. use 'anywhere', 'anyone', 'anything' with a negative verb, not 'nowhere', 'no one', 'nothing'.
english has 12 pure vowel sounds and 8 diphthongs. the vowel system is much larger than in many other languages, making it challenging for learners.
english has 24 consonant sounds. some of these (like /θ/, /ð/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ŋ/) do not exist in arabic and require special attention.
english has irregular verbs, exceptions, and idioms — even native speakers make mistakes.
english is a stress-timed language. content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) are stressed; function words (prepositions, articles, pronouns) are reduced. this creates the rhythm of english.

english uses 'would', 'could', 'may', and 'might' to soften requests and make them more polite. these modal verbs in conditional form are much more polite than direct imperatives. 'could' is the most common for requests; 'may' is the most formal.

english uses at, in, and on for both time and place. at = specific points (at 5 pm, at the door). in = larger areas/periods (in cairo, in summer). on = surfaces/dates (on the table, on monday). this is very different from arabic prepositions.

for a missing word, explain plainly and continue: “the tool that measures the amount” may communicate the idea until you recall scale. a short correction such as “last month—actually, last winter” can protect a relevant fact. replacing a clear word repeatedly can disrupt the message more than keeping it.
for a physical skill i would choose a workshop because someone can notice a mistake before it becomes a habit. an online tutorial is useful later when i need to review the steps.

for a plan, locate fixed reference points and update the traveller’s direction. for a lecture, record definitions, mechanisms, examples and limitations. for an announcement, separate change, continuity and required action. one rule such as choose the final number cannot answer all these demands.

for a practical notice, mark action, person, time and condition. ‘applications require references unless you have completed the internal course’ contains a broad rule and an exception. the exception cannot be ignored just because references is easy to find. two candidates can need different actions under the same notice.

for a report on the newsletter trial, turn a finding into an action: outdated event details → assign a final fact check → review correction requests after publication. for a review, explain the value and limitation to a student reader rather than issue instructions to a manager. these are different paragraph purposes.

for a return question, before four is relevant; noon to two governs collection. up to three working days gives a maximum, not an automatic three-day entitlement in every situation. an extension request must be timely and remains conditional. a faithful checklist says collect in the stated window / return by the due time / request extension before the due date / await approval.
for a school-uniform question: cost → reuse scheme; identity → shared appearance; own point → comfort and movement.

for a study routine, ‘i break a large assignment into small tasks’ states the method. ‘it lets me find missing evidence before the final day’ explains its benefit. a presentation example then shows the mechanism in action. an unrelated account of a holiday may be fluent but does not support the answer.

for a three-stage prompt “restore the complete word: caref___”, enter careful. do not enter only ul. an optional drill explicitly asking for missing letters after caref would instead require ul; read the particular input instruction. the activity deliberately reviews a whole-word response in one box; it does not reproduce the official missing-letter interface or adaptive sequencing.
for a tight travel connection, name one verified fact to check and one contingency. does the photo establish any test-centre requirement?

for a workshop moved from tuesday room 6 to thursday room 9, keep separate entries for date and room. if the start remains 2 pm, do not replace it with a later number that refers to a reply deadline. existing registrations remaining valid means attendance does not require a new registration unless the announcement says so.
for adults who are comfortable walking it was excellent.
for american accents, use npr. for australian accents, use abc news australia.
for an action that started in the past and continues, use present perfect continuous (have been living) or present perfect (have lived).

for an open future condition, present simple often appears after if and a modal appears in the result clause. a more hypothetical condition may use a different pattern. the forms express the speaker’s viewpoint on the possibility, rather than mechanically identifying a calendar time.

for an unfamiliar organiser, start with a purpose and a specific information gap: “i am considering the evening language class. could you confirm whether ___?” embedded questions use statement order: “whether beginners can join”, not “whether can beginners join”. courtesy should make the request easy to answer.

for anyone wanting a quiet place to read, the oak room is reserved for silent use. the willow room allows group discussion but must be booked. the cedar room contains computers and a printer, although printing requires credit on your account. the birch room has art materials and is open only when a tutor is present.
for band 7+: use sufficient range for flexibility and precision, use less common vocabulary with awareness of style and collocation.
for build a sentence, language use is the primary criterion — must be grammatically correct.

for c, write the two headings your plan needs. check: reasons for free entry; evaluation of whether the policy is positive. add one access benefit and one funding concern, then explain your judgement.
for candidates needing moderate improvement (band 5.5 to 6.5 or 6.0 to 7.0). requires 2-3 hours daily. the most commonly recommended timeline.
for candidates needing significant improvement (band 4.5-5.0 to 6.5+) or more preparation time. requires 1.5-2 hours daily.
for candidates with strong english skills (band 6.0-6.5) needing familiarisation with test format and strategies. requires 3-4 hours daily.

for contextual reading, keep answers and source explanations. for listening, use actual audio before transcript review. for build a sentence, preserve the reconstructed clause and explain its grammar. for email and discussion, save full responses and identify coverage and development. for repetition and interview, use actual speech with word-accuracy and delivery review.
for conversations, label which speaker said what. note attitudes with symbols.
for dessert, we had chocolate cake.
for each article, practice summarising paragraphs, identifying opinion, and noting vocabulary.
for each error type, write the correct rule in your own words.

for each gap, name the complete expression or sentence role first. explain the difference between selecting the collocation and changing its word-family form. read the complete source and answer each question. use only the evidence given. these are original lesson tasks, not a complete examination paper.

for each option ask: who or what is involved, what happened, when, and how certain is it? a passage about complaints on four streets cannot establish an effect on every street in a city. fewer complaints do not automatically mean fewer accidents. an option can be wrong in one component even when its other words closely resemble the source.

for each prompt, compare the original sentence with your actual recording. first mark omitted, substituted, added or reordered words. then listen for a key ending, preposition or condition that became unclear. similar meaning is insufficient for exact repetition, and a reason or personal example should not be added. rehearse the difficult group, place it back in the complete sentence and test new audio. the model transcribes the intended wording; it does not automatically assess your pronunciation or award an official score.

for each task, label one required point that a weak response might omit. check: the email may forget a feasible solution; the discussion may favour free access without explaining how necessary costs are handled.

for every wrong answer, record question demand → source clause → your interpretation → corrected interpretation. if the source does not discuss a proposed outcome, do not treat missing information as proof of the opposite. a condition after only or unless can change the action for a particular reader.

for example usually introduces an illustration, whereas because points toward a reason and however can introduce a qualification. signals help orient you, but the following clause supplies the content. ‘however, young trees need watering’ limits a practical proposal; it does not mean shade has no effect.
for example, ... has been shown to improve ...
for example: missing keys → retrace café visit → staff return them → now use a secure pocket. develop your own details rather than claiming the model as a personal experience.

for example: require a short explanation of the change so the learner connects revision to a reason. “this will eradicate all mistakes” overstates the effect. plain help or improve is suitable when it expresses the limited claim accurately.

for example: the certificate needs the correct surname; ask whether the record can be corrected; provide the enrolment reference. “you have corrected it” would claim a completed action rather than make the request.
for example: tutor / project deadline / smaller steps / weekly plan / finished calmly. your own conversation can differ; the final note should explain its effect.

for example: “a charge can reduce some unnecessary car journeys when a practical alternative exists, but it may add difficulty for travellers who have no usable route.” the answer distinguishes groups and conditions instead of abandoning judgement.

for example: “a charge might encourage customers to bring a bag because they would avoid paying again.” customers can bring; they would avoid supplies a complete reason clause. check relevance and grammar, not whether you reproduced these exact words.

for example: “although the museum extended its hours, some workers still could not attend.” “the visitors who need assistance wait at reception.” both clauses have clear subjects and finite verbs. other completions are valid if meaning and agreement remain coherent.

for example: “an exhibition may need additional loans and supervision. a short event could therefore use a separate ticket to cover part of those costs. however, the price and what it includes should remain clear.” the weak version repeats an evaluation without explaining what the money supports.

for example: “barriers to continued attendance rather than assume the timetable suits everyone.” universal dislike is not reported. asking for feedback is an investigation, not a finding about what every visitor thought.

for example: “could you check the return record for atlas reference a16? i placed it in the returns box on tuesday afternoon and can bring my loan receipt.” the request identifies a practical check without assuming the outcome.

for example: “could you exchange it for the edition listed on my order? i can return the unused copy, provided you explain the return procedure. please confirm whether a replacement can arrive before the course begins.” it gives action and practical constraints without assuming approval.

for example: “during my visit, i had to leave the changing area to ask for help. this would be difficult for a first-time visitor because the payment system is unfamiliar. i would recommend asking at reception before changing.” the action addresses the stated limitation.

for example: “editing takes staff time, so the college could begin with one short digital issue. this would protect time for checking facts while showing whether students read it.” the weak sentence repeats its evaluation without explaining how the information helps a reader.
for example: “from unrestricted donations to documented collection.” unlabelled photographs identifies the middle problem but misses both the earlier policy and the resulting change.

for example: “i agree that a quiet room would help exam candidates, although it would remove space from shared activities. how could we preserve room for both?” the invitation concerns a trade-off and permits a real response; it is more useful than “do you agree?” repeated after every sentence.

for example: “i enjoy baking because i can make something for other people.” other activities are valid. “because useful” leaves the reason incomplete here; “because it is useful” supplies a subject and verb but still benefits from explaining useful in what way.

for example: “i had never recognised mint by smell until i joined the balcony herb class. beginners handle a few safe kitchen herbs and learn how to grow them in small containers.” the concrete discovery creates interest and the second sentence explains the activity. other natural openings are valid.

for example: “i like the journey because it gives me twenty quiet minutes to read before work.” the reason explains value rather than repeating the noun. add a real example only if it supports that value.

for example: “if you need a place to talk between classes, look for a seating area with room for a small group.” develop the layout or available seats. opening hours, prices and noise would need separate evidence.

for example: “other student support also needs funding. it could begin by offering a one-term subsidy to a defined group. this would allow staff to check demand and attendance before expanding it.” cycle stands may be worthwhile, but they do not directly resolve how the bus subsidy is funded.

for example: “pages six and seven are missing the diagrams needed for our comparison. could you send a complete accessible copy by friday afternoon?” the revision identifies the problem, purpose and response needed without an accusation.

for example: “repeatedly using the same bag reduces the number of disposable bags needed. a reminder near the entrance could help regular shoppers remember to bring one.” the additional own idea, such as cost, is still missing until developed separately.

for example: “some / was / evidence.” research names an activity or body of investigation here; studies counts separate investigations. specialised uses exist, but the ordinary academic frames in these tasks use research as uncountable.

for example: “some beginners avoid a court because they do not know how to join a game. a supervised introductory session could show them the basic routine, provided staffing is available.” other reasons work if they explain participation rather than simply praise sport.

for example: “the bench is surrounded by greenery / which would give me a pleasant view / during a reading break.” the groups preserve connected ideas without breaking up a noun phrase. quietness, public access and comfort would need experience or other information, rather than being facts established by the photograph.

for example: “the pilot suggests a possible benefit in the classes studied.” guarantee removes uncertainty and every class widens the population. both changes require more evidence than the pilot provides.
for example: “the preliminary report provides limited findings, with two sites still to be examined.” a preliminary label cannot make an unsupported universal guarantee accurate.

for example: “their shifts change weekly. offering a choice of two sessions would help by allowing attendance around work. however, teacher workload would still need attention.” the weak evaluation explains neither low attendance nor a targeted response.

for example: “this timetable change helped visitors, but it created a transport problem for some stallholders.” but or however signals the trade-off. a result connector would incorrectly make the benefit itself the explanation for every later difficulty.

for example: “transport and handling can add costs absent from the quoted item price.” totals require relevant amounts and quantities. distant supply is not automatically cheaper or more expensive in every case.

for example: “we grouped the labels by date, which let us match each one to the correct display. visitors could then follow the sequence.” the action explains the result instead of simply announcing success.

for fresh practice, ask someone to read two short reviews without showing the text. identify which part is accepted and which judgement survives the qualification. check the transcript only after responding. if the words were heard correctly but the evaluation was reversed, practise interpreting concessions rather than increasing playback speed.

for fresh sentences, reconstruct the full version after reduction. verify actor, sequence, cause and voice. later, write a sentence that should remain unreduced and explain the ambiguity a shorter form would create.
for general training review: evidence and next steps, write 60–90 words identifying one concrete difficulty from a previous activity and a relevant follow-up. avoid assigning yourself a band.

for ielts academic, typical requirements are: undergraduate programs 6.0-6.5 overall, postgraduate programs 6.5-7.0 overall, and professional programs (medicine, nursing, law, teaching) 7.0-7.5 overall. ielts general training for migration typically requires 6.0-7.0 in each band depending on the country and visa type.
for ielts general training task 1 (150 words, 20 minutes).
for increases: rise, increase, grow, climb, surge, soar, rocket. for decreases: fall, decrease, drop, decline, plummet, plunge.

for independent rehearsal, write three short profiles sharing a topic but differing in one decisive condition. ask a partner to select for a specified learner. if two profiles genuinely satisfy every condition, the question needs revision; adding an arbitrary preference after checking is not fair evidence.
for inference questions, look for the answer that must be true based on the passage, not just possibly true.
for integrated tasks, accurate representation of source materials and clear relationship between them is essential.
for introduces a duration; present perfect connects past to now.

for live lecture gaps, predict the note role, listen, then transfer exact words if requested. personal arrow notes may paraphrase the mechanism, but a source-word response must follow its stated rule. these are separate operations.

for live passages, distinguish unit price, additional costs and total cost. where the source offers several additional costs, a response can name a supported one within the word limit. check whether the question requests one supported cost or every cost before deciding how much to include.
for maps showing change: was demolished, was built, was converted into, was replaced by, was extended.

for maps, ‘a playground replaced the lawn’ and ‘the lawn was replaced by a playground’ describe the same change with different subjects. ‘the playground was replaced by a lawn’ reverses it. for a general process, ‘workers sort the paper’ and ‘the paper is sorted’ focus on different participants; use the passive when the supplied material is the main thread.
for maps: to the north of, south of, adjacent to, in the centre of, opposite, on the opposite side of.
for my usual route, i generally choose the train over the bus because the journey is quicker. this does not mean the train is faster on every route.

for process diagrams: introduction paraphrases, overview states number of stages, body 1 covers first half of stages, body 2 covers remaining stages. for maps: overview describes most significant change, body 1 describes earlier layout, body 2 describes later layout.
for processes: the process begins with, next, then, after that, subsequently, finally, the process concludes with.
for pronunciation, focus on clarity. identify difficult english sounds and practice them.
for prose summary, eliminate options that mention specific details, examples, or statistics.
for sentence insertion, try inserting at each marked position and evaluate logical flow.

for several months, karim arrived at work feeling as if his day had already begun too quickly. his journey was not especially long, but he filled every minute with messages, news and short videos. one morning, his phone battery ran out before he reached the station. at first, the silence felt inconvenient. he kept reaching for a device that could no longer entertain him.
for significant improvement from lower english level (toefl 60-70 target). 1.5-2 hours daily, 5 days per week.

for sparse dated values, avoid claiming a smooth curve or unshown peak. ‘increased between the recorded dates’ states the supplied comparison without inventing what happened in each intermediate month. precise ordinary language is stronger than dramatic trend vocabulary unsupported by the visual.
for stability: remained stable, stayed constant, levelled off, plateaued, fluctuated.
for test-takers near their target score needing format familiarization. 3-4 hours daily, 6 days per week.
for that reason, the jury found the defendant guilty.
for that reason. formed from 'there' + 'fore'. indicates a logical conclusion.

for the announcement assessment, attach deadlines to their actions. an event date, response deadline and opening time can all be true. review each missed answer by naming the task-specific failure: orientation, copied word, mechanism, attribution or action status. then practise that step on unfamiliar audio.

for the beginner needing weekend access and supplied equipment, a meets all three conditions. b matches the weekend but fails equipment and entry level. c supplies materials and may introduce techniques, but its meeting day fails the weekend requirement. to match ‘appreciated time to revise’, a again supplies explicit support. to match ‘found repeated instruction unnecessary’, c fits; its repetition was not experienced as a benefit.

for the course booking, preview only the printed fields and leave their values empty. for the repair and reservation recordings, make your own notes rather than carrying over the rehearsal categories. read a unit already printed beside the gap before entering an amount.

for the email, state the problem and request a room change. for the discussion, take a position and support it with a relevant reason.

for the first sentence: “visitors who arrive after the tour begins / should wait near reception.” the relative clause identifies late arrivals; omitting it wrongly turns the direction into one for all visitors. in the second sentence, the main gallery is closed but the upper-floor exhibition remains open; changing “although” to “because” changes the relationship.

for the first two live speakers, draw two rows and three empty columns: expectation, reported experience, final judgement. do not assign a statement until the speaker’s turn is complete. before moving to the five-speaker stage, cover the column titles and decide which two notes you actually need.

for the fresh live conversations, use empty option / constraint / status notes first, then reduce them to your own short cues. after checking, name the exact failed requirement or status change. later, retrieve the difference between asking permission and receiving confirmation on a new exchange.

for the guided recording, identify the missing information before looking at options. for later exchanges, listen to the whole utterance and decide whether it requests information, help, confirmation or consideration of a suggestion. do not force every item into “final decision”.

for the independent funding question, write your own reasons before reopening the sports essay. mark position, explanation, example, limitation and conclusion only where they occur. do not assume that a local sports barrier or the model’s priority also applies to cultural events.

for the live changed-appointment and workshop tasks, preserve only facts actually given in their prompts and recordings. do not invent a clinic or extra equipment. written-study mode is preparation; actual speech and a listener or qualified reviewer are needed to judge intelligibility.

for the live interviews, use your own experience and answer every requested action. after replay, ask whether the restated question kept the same learner, options and demand. later, make a fresh comparison without a sentence frame.

for the live longer sets, check wording and actual delivery separately. after another module, try a fresh once-heard sentence with a condition. a smoother reading of the old transcript demonstrates rehearsal; it does not establish retention of new audio.

for the live messages, check each required point against your own draft, not the reading-pack model. underline the action the recipient can take. later, revise one vague request from another email by naming its object, timing and practical alternative. a courteous greeting cannot compensate for missing content.

for the live notices, mark required action, permission, deadline and exception. in the independent stage, create your own rule map. after checking, explain the exact condition lost in a wrong choice and revisit it with a fresh practical notice later.

for the live recordings, first note the speaker’s final judgement and supporting clause, leaving the label blank until the turn finishes. in the next source, choose your own brief notes. after feedback, identify the nearest wrong summary’s lost qualifier or incorrect speaker.

for the live schemes and four-year series, calculate their actual changes and compare rank separately. a smaller category can grow faster while remaining smaller. for the research-method comparison, choose the method from purpose and limitation rather than calling one universally best.

for the live token tasks, use every supplied piece and respect the fixed boundaries and punctuation conditions. later, reconstruct a new clause from your own notes without tokens to test production beyond the exact-order adaptation.

for the reminder assessment, reason about the stated possible effect and a limiting condition rather than copy the whole adoption essay. after the next writing task, retrieve the difference between explaining a mechanism and weighing its importance.

for the supplied transport table, write “overall, ___ led among students, whereas ___ led among staff.” then group non-car comparisons rather than walking through every cell without a point. a full model follows after this attempt.

for the technician and induction emails, make a short coverage plan and develop each required action into a clear sentence or paragraph. after review, repair one vague pronoun or missing alternative. later, write a new actionable request without the supplied problem/consequence/action labels.

for the theatre recording, make an empty aim / achieved gain note. for the beekeeper interview, choose your own brief role labels from the questions rather than the written demonstration. the boat-restoration assessment changes the activity and demand again.

for the tutor, begin with the project and reason, then propose a bounded extension and show how work will continue. complete “the archive closure prevents me from ___, but i can still ___. would it be possible to ___?” respect the tutor’s decision; do not write that the deadline has already changed.

for two methods, ‘a is faster but less precise than b’ compares the same dimensions. ‘a has more speed’ may be understandable, but the direct comparative is usually clearer. if purpose determines the choice, state the condition: use a for rapid preliminary checks and b when precision matters.

for urban cooling, shade and evaporation are mechanisms. ‘shade reduces sunlight reaching a pavement’ develops the first; ‘water leaving foliage uses energy’ develops the second. species, maturity and root space are conditions. notes such as trees / water / space preserve vocabulary but lose which idea explains which.
for weak changes: edge up, creep up, dip, edge down, taper off.

for why services move online, a mechanism could be lower routine administrative work: users choose available appointments directly rather than waiting for a telephone operator. for how to avoid exclusion, identify who cannot benefit from that route and why. a telephone alternative helps someone without internet; clearer labels may help someone confused by navigation; neither is a universal cure.
for your next email, write each section label on a separate line before filling in the content.

for your own vocabulary record, store a base, two useful forms and one sentence for each, rather than a translation alone. after a wrong response, label the cause: role, meaning, number or spelling. then write a new sentence using the corrected form. being able to explain why a form fits a new sentence is stronger evidence of learning than recognising the same answer again.

for “could you tell me where to collect the forms?”, “at the science office opposite the stairs” supplies a location. “yes, i collected one yesterday” repeats the activity but does not answer where. for “would you mind checking...?”, “of course—send the draft” accepts the request.
for “should shops charge for disposable bags?”, write a position and one sentence explaining how a charge might affect a shopper’s decision.

for “the guide will meet visitors near the information desk”, possible memory groups are “the guide / will meet visitors / near the information desk”. the required repetition is the original sentence. “a guide meets people by a desk” conveys a related idea but substitutes wording and changes grammatical detail.
for “what would you like to learn to cook?”, which opening answers directly: “i cooked pasta yesterday” or “i would like to learn to bake bread”? explain the time difference.

formal, semi-formal and informal choices affect greetings, phrasing and closings, but useful content remains essential in each. a clear request can be courteous without being obscure. in a task with several content points, each contributes to achieving the letter’s purpose.

formal-sounding words are not inherently more precise. a measured verb or a clearly limited claim can communicate the intended meaning better than inflated certainty. the response’s development comes from explaining how an idea works, with language suited to a classroom discussion.
