section 2 is a monologue in a social context. this might be a guide giving information about a museum, a manager explaining company policies, a radio announcer describing a local event, or someone giving directions.

section 3 is a conversation between up to four speakers in an academic context. this typically involves students discussing a project, a tutorial with a professor, or students preparing a presentation. questions often test understanding of opinions, attitudes, and the development of the discussion.

section 4 is an academic lecture or talk. a single speaker presents on an academic topic such as environmental science, business studies, archaeology, or public health. this is the most challenging section because of the complex vocabulary, dense information, and sustained focus required.

shops should stop giving away single-use bags, although customers still need a practical way to carry unexpected purchases. a gradual change would be more helpful than simply removing every option overnight. the main environmental benefit comes from using fewer bags. a customer who keeps a sturdy bag and brings it on later visits does not need a new one each time. however, buying another reusable bag on every trip would weaken that benefit. convenience remains a reasonable concern. someone buying food after work may not have planned the visit. shops could offer an inexpensive reusable bag and remind regular customers to bring one. this would preserve a solution without encouraging unlimited disposable use. cost also matters. a charge should encourage a change in habit rather than make an ordinary shopping trip unnecessarily expensive. overall, i support ending free disposable bags if shops explain the change and provide an affordable alternative.

some people argue that employers should provide training whenever workers need new skills, while others believe employees should take responsibility for their own development. i think responsibility should be shared, with the balance depending on who benefits and whether the training is required for the job. employers should normally provide instruction that workers need to perform their current duties safely and effectively. if a company introduces new equipment, it controls both the decision and the working conditions. expecting employees to learn alone could lead to inconsistent practice and avoidable mistakes. paid training time also makes participation possible for workers who have caring responsibilities or limited resources outside work. employees nevertheless have a role in identifying their learning needs and using opportunities actively. a course will achieve little if participants do not practise or ask about difficulties. workers may also choose to develop skills for a different career, and it would be unreasonable to expect their present employer to fund every personal ambition. in those cases, public education or individual study may be more appropriate. a practical arrangement would begin with a discussion of the skill required, the expected benefit and the support needed. the employer could provide time and essential resources, while the employee agrees on a realistic learning plan and applies the new skill. progress should be reviewed through actual work rather than attendance alone. in conclusion, neither complete employer responsibility nor complete individual responsibility is convincing. training linked directly to current work should be supported by the organisation, while employees should participate thoughtfully and take initiative. clear agreements are more useful than broad claims that one side must bear every cost.

some towns spend large sums on major cultural events, while smaller neighbourhood activities receive less attention. i believe both can have value, but local authorities should give priority to activities that residents can use regularly and that remain affordable to maintain. a large festival can attract visitors and create opportunities for local businesses. it may also bring residents together around a shared experience. these benefits are strongest when local people can participate rather than simply watch an event designed mainly for tourists. however, a brief increase in visitor numbers does not establish a lasting improvement in community life. regular neighbourhood activities offer a different advantage. a weekly repair group, reading club or accessible sports session creates repeated contact between people who might otherwise remain strangers. this can build trust gradually and provide practical support. such activities may be less visible than a major festival, yet their value should not be judged only by publicity or attendance on one day. funding decisions should therefore consider access, continuity and realistic staffing. a programme that depends on a few exhausted volunteers may not survive even if its initial event is popular. the council could support modest activities in existing buildings and review participation before expanding them. larger events could still receive funding when their wider benefits are clearly explained and essential local services are protected. in conclusion, a balanced cultural programme need not reject major occasions. nevertheless, regular opportunities for residents to learn, meet and participate should form its foundation. public money is more likely to create lasting value when success is defined through meaningful access and sustainable activity rather than a single impressive crowd.

source: ‘i would support the evening service if transport were available. at present the last bus leaves too early, so i am not ready to recommend it for everyone.’ the speaker sees a possible benefit but withholds a universal recommendation. ‘strongly rejects all evening services’ is too negative. ‘fully supports the current arrangement’ loses the unresolved access problem.

source: ‘the panels are removable: maintenance staff can lift them out to reach the wall.’ removable means capable of being taken away or detached in this context. the explanation after the colon constrains the meaning; you do not need specialist construction knowledge. ‘permanent’ would contradict the described action.

source: ‘tuesday would suit me, but the room is booked. thursday is possible if the technician can attend. i have checked with her, and friday is now confirmed.’ tuesday is rejected; thursday remains a conditional possibility in the account; friday is confirmed. notes should preserve those statuses, not simply list the days.

source: ‘volunteers map drinking fountains using an old list. a location is marked verified only after a recent visit. reports of faults are checked before an update. the organisers advise carrying water on longer walks because conditions may change.’ detail: verification needs a visit. procedure: a report is not automatically published. overall position: the map is useful assistance, not a guarantee.

source: “heavy rain damaged the outdoor stage. ___. several families therefore asked to transfer their tickets.” choose between “the organisers moved the performance to a weekday afternoon” and “many people enjoyed last year’s performance.” the first sentence creates a problem; the final sentence reports a consequence requiring a new explanation.

source: “the delivery arrives thursday morning; tell reception by wednesday at four if you cannot be there.” complete event → ___; contact deadline → ___; group requiring contact → ___. then explain what is unknown about the delivery’s precise hour.

source: “the inventory was provisional: staff expected to revise it after checking the remaining boxes.” replace provisional with not final, then reread. “based only on guesses” adds a claim the definition does not supply.

source: “the path was poorly marked, so several walkers lost their way. the signs were ___ (help). after receiving three written ___ (complain), the owner replaced them.” first find the consequence, then the number cue. do not automatically choose a positive adjective because a root seems positive.

technology has made home working possible for many occupations, and i believe its advantages can outweigh its disadvantages when organisations manage it carefully. the benefit is flexibility rather than the assumption that every job should become remote. a major advantage is the reduction in unnecessary travel. workers can use time previously spent commuting for rest, family responsibilities or focused work. employers may also recruit people who live farther away or have difficulty attending an office every day. these gains can widen access to employment, provided the role can genuinely be performed remotely and the worker has suitable equipment. the disadvantages concern both working conditions and communication. a home may lack a quiet space, and the boundary between work and personal time can become unclear. employees may feel expected to answer messages throughout the evening. informal learning is also harder when beginners cannot easily observe experienced colleagues or ask a brief question. these problems would make unrestricted remote working unsuitable as a universal rule. however, they can be reduced through clear arrangements. employers should define availability, provide appropriate support and create deliberate opportunities for collaboration. some teams may benefit from a hybrid pattern, while others can work remotely with scheduled contact. the decision should reflect the task and the employee’s circumstances rather than a desire to treat every worker identically. in conclusion, technology-enabled home working offers substantial advantages in time and access, but those benefits depend on reasonable boundaries and effective communication. i therefore favour it as a supported option rather than a compulsory replacement for workplaces. under those conditions, the flexibility it creates is likely to be more valuable than the difficulties it introduces.

the changing life of a public building the old market hall in alderwick has served several purposes since trading moved elsewhere. it was used for storage, stood empty for years and later became a venue for occasional events. each phase left traces in the building, from repaired doorways to marks showing where temporary partitions had stood. a current proposal would turn it into a community workshop and exhibition space. supporters describe this as a return to the hall’s original role as a meeting place. the phrase is appealing, but the building’s history is less simple. trading brought people together, yet access and influence were not shared equally. a new public use should therefore be judged by present needs rather than by an idealised account of the past. the survey has identified practical questions. the roof needs repairs, and the main entrance includes steps. an accessible entrance could be created on the east side, but this would affect the layout of one proposed workshop. organisers also need a realistic plan for heating and staffing during quieter months. none of these issues means the project should be abandoned. they show why a useful feasibility study must go beyond an attractive picture of a finished building. a phased approach could begin with a safe, accessible section and expand once demand is clearer. the hall’s history offers possibilities, not a guarantee that every proposed activity will succeed. a phased plan also has risks. an unfinished appearance could make residents doubt whether the project will ever be completed, while repeated building work may disrupt early users. organisers propose publishing a sequence of achievable stages, with a clear explanation of what each stage would provide. this would allow the public to distinguish a limited first opening from a promise that every proposed facility is already available. consultation has revealed differences in expected use. some residents want classes led by qualified tutors, while others mainly need affordable space for groups they organise themselves. both could fit the building, but they imply different staffing and booking arrangements. the project team has therefore resisted treating a large number of expressions of interest as proof of one uniform demand. it will ask what people would attend, when they could come and what they could reasonably pay. these practical questions connect the building’s history with its future without pretending that the past supplies a complete answer. preserving a market hall can protect a distinctive part of the town, but preservation should enable useful access rather than turn the building into a symbol that residents cannot afford to use. the writer’s support remains conditional on a plan that explains both its ambitions and its limits.

the line graph compares the proportion of electricity produced from renewable energy sources across four european nations—germany, the united kingdom, spain, and italy—over a fourteen-year period from 2010 to 2024. overall, all four countries witnessed significant growth in their renewable electricity portfolios. germany and the uk demonstrated the most precipitous upward trajectories, with germany overtaking spain to secure the highest renewable share by 2024, whereas italy experienced the most modest net expansion. in 2010, spain was the clear leader, generating approximately 32% of its electricity from renewables, followed by italy at 22% and germany at 17%. the uk registered the lowest baseline figure, producing a mere 7%. over the subsequent fourteen years, the uk experienced dramatic exponential acceleration, quadrupling to reach 33% in 2018 before climbing to 48% by 2024. germany exhibited steady, robust gains throughout the period, rising from 17% in 2010 to 38% in 2018, before surging to surpass spain and finish at 56% in 2024. spain maintained a steady upward incline to reach 51%, while italy's growth plateaued around 2014–2018 before concluding at 39%, the lowest of the four nations by the end of the survey.

the line graph compares the proportions of all trips made by bicycle and bus in norford at four points between 2010 and 2025. overall, cycling became more common throughout the period, whereas the share of bus travel declined. buses accounted for a much larger proportion initially, but bicycles had overtaken them by the final year shown. in 2010, 10% of trips were made by bicycle, compared with 40% by bus. the cycling figure rose to 15% in 2015 and then increased more rapidly, reaching 25% in 2020 and 35% in 2025. its overall gain was therefore 25 percentage points. bus travel followed the opposite pattern. its share fell slightly to 38% in 2015, then declined to 35% in 2020 and 30% in 2025. the gap between the two modes narrowed from 30 percentage points at the start to ten in 2020. by 2025, cycling exceeded bus travel by five points. the graph gives proportions rather than total trip numbers.

the pervasive ascendancy of e-commerce has fundamentally reshaped retail habits over the past two decades. while millions of consumers celebrate the unmatched convenience and price competitiveness of online marketplaces, community advocates warn that the hollowed-out high street threatens social cohesion and localized economic vitality. in this essay, i will consider both sides of this development before presenting my own view that while digital commerce is irreversible, town centres must reinvent themselves to survive. proponents of e-commerce point to overwhelming consumer benefits. digital platforms allow individuals to compare prices, browse global inventories, and receive home deliveries with a single keystroke. for working parents, the elderly, or rural residents who lack access to extensive urban shopping centres, online retail saves substantial time and fuel costs. furthermore, algorithmic logistics and reduced overheads enable companies to offer lower consumer prices, dampening household inflationary pressure. conversely, the erosion of physical retail stores incurs steep socioeconomic costs. high streets have traditionally served as vital communal hubs where citizens interact, fostering neighborhood familiarity and trust. when small, family-owned boutiques shutter, towns lose unique cultural character, and low-skilled employment opportunities disappear. moreover, abandoned storefronts induce urban decay, deterring tourism and diminishing local property tax revenues that fund public services like schools and libraries. in my perspective, the shift towards online retail cannot and should not be forcibly reversed; convenience will always triumph in a market economy. however, local councils must assist high streets in transitioning from pure transactional commodity spaces into social, experiential destinations—such as pedestrianized cultural quarters, artisanal markets, and dining spaces. by doing so, communities can preserve social vibrancy while still reaping the logistical efficiencies of digital commerce.

the phenomenon of globalisation has fundamentally reshaped the cultural landscape of the twenty-first century, facilitating an unprecedented flow of people, ideas, and practices across national borders. as migration patterns intensify and digital connectivity erodes geographical barriers, societies around the world are becoming increasingly multicultural. this transformation presents both extraordinary opportunities and formidable challenges for social cohesion.

the return of a neighbourhood workshop the workshop on milton road began as a place where residents could borrow tools. its organisers soon discovered that access to equipment was only one part of the need. some members did not know which tool suited a task, while others were confident using it but uncertain about safety checks. the group introduced short demonstrations and a system allowing beginners to work beside experienced volunteers. this slowed some sessions, yet it made the workshop more welcoming. members were encouraged to explain what they were trying to achieve before choosing equipment, which sometimes revealed that a simpler method would be safer. as attendance grew, the organisers faced pressure to open more often. they resisted an immediate expansion because a few volunteers were already carrying most of the responsibility. a survey asked members which additional session would be most useful and whether they could contribute time. the resulting rota added one evening without requiring the same people to supervise every week. the workshop also kept a record of repairs that could not be completed. these failures helped identify missing skills and unavailable parts. they were not removed from the annual report simply to make the project appear more successful. the writer argues that a community service develops through careful attention to limits as well as enthusiasm. the workshop’s value lies in shared knowledge and practical access, but maintaining that value requires training, realistic staffing and honest reporting. a larger programme would not necessarily be a better one if it exhausted the people keeping it open. an additional debate concerned membership fees. some volunteers argued that a higher fee would provide stable income and reduce the need to apply for small grants. others worried that the people most likely to benefit from borrowing equipment might be the least able to pay. the group introduced a standard fee with a confidential reduced-rate option, while continuing to seek support for training. this did not remove the financial uncertainty, but it made the trade-off visible. the organisers were also careful about the language of independence. their aim was not to suggest that every resident should become an expert or that asking for professional help represented failure. some repairs require specialist knowledge, and knowing when to stop can be as valuable as learning a new technique. a notice beside the workbench explained which jobs the volunteers could support and which should be referred elsewhere. looking ahead, the group plans to review who uses the workshop as well as how often it opens. if attendance grows mainly among already confident members, a larger timetable may not improve access for beginners. the next evaluation will therefore include short conversations with people who joined once and did not return. their experience could reveal barriers that regular users no longer notice. expansion remains possible, but it will follow evidence about need and capacity rather than become a measure of success in itself.

the value of a negative result research reports tend to attract attention when a new treatment or method appears to work. a finding that an intervention produced no measurable improvement may seem less newsworthy, yet it can prevent others from repeating an ineffective approach. the absence of an observed effect also needs careful interpretation. a study may be too small, too short or too imprecise to detect a change that exists. in a trial of classroom lighting, researchers found no clear difference in test performance between two settings. they had measured only one kind of task during a single afternoon. it would therefore be unreasonable to conclude that lighting never affects learning. the result supported a narrower statement: under the tested conditions, this particular change did not produce a detectable difference on that task. publishing the method and uncertainty allowed another team to design a longer study. that team could avoid repeating the same limitations and could choose measures more closely related to fatigue. the initial result was therefore useful even without a positive effect. the writer argues that researchers should describe both what their evidence permits and what remains unresolved. treating a negative result as failure encourages exaggerated claims and hides useful information. equally, calling every inconclusive result proof of no effect would be a different mistake. progress depends on clear questions, transparent methods and conclusions no broader than the evidence supports. the distinction becomes especially important when results enter public discussion. a headline saying that a method does not work is simpler than an explanation of uncertainty, but it may discourage a useful follow-up study. the opposite headline, claiming that a small unresolved effect proves success, would be equally misleading. researchers cannot control every summary of their work, yet they can make the limits clear in the report itself. a well-described negative result can also improve decisions about resources. if several careful studies fail to find the benefit a programme was designed to produce, continuing it unchanged becomes harder to justify. that conclusion depends on the combined evidence, not merely on one unsuccessful afternoon. it may lead to revising the intervention, changing the outcome measured or choosing a different approach. the writer therefore separates openness to new evidence from a refusal to make decisions. uncertainty does not mean that all options are equally supported. it means that a decision should reflect the strength of the available evidence and remain open to revision. publishing methods and results, including those that are disappointing, allows others to understand that judgement and build on it.

today we will consider how shade affects city streets. trees can reduce direct sunlight on paving, but their benefits vary with canopy size and water availability. a young tree does not immediately provide the same cooling as a mature one. researchers therefore record canopy cover as well as tree numbers. they also distinguish surface temperature from air temperature, since a cooler pavement does not necessarily mean an identical reduction in the air around it. for planning, maintenance matters: a planting programme without reliable watering may lose trees before they establish.

today we will look at how plants respond to limited water. one visible response is wilting, but important changes may occur before leaves lose their shape. some plants close tiny openings on their leaves, reducing water loss. those openings also allow gases to move in and out, so closing them can restrict the carbon dioxide available for photosynthesis. the response therefore involves a trade-off rather than a cost-free solution. researchers comparing species must consider when and where they grow. a plant adapted to brief dry periods may respond differently from one that regularly faces long droughts. in an experiment, giving all plants the same amount of water does not necessarily create the same degree of stress, because leaf area and root systems vary. measurements should match the question being asked. if we want to understand survival, a short-term change in growth is relevant but not sufficient on its own.

today’s topic is peatland restoration. peat forms when plant material decomposes slowly in waterlogged conditions. draining the land changes those conditions and allows stored carbon to be released. restoration often begins by blocking drainage channels, but water levels must be monitored rather than assumed to recover immediately.

urban streams are often treated as drains, yet they are also habitats. when rain falls on roofs and roads, water reaches the stream more quickly than it would through soil. this can produce a sudden increase in flow, carrying pollutants and disturbing organisms. one response is to create planted areas that temporarily hold rainwater. these areas slow the movement of water, although their capacity is limited during prolonged storms. researchers assessing a project should measure both the amount of water retained and how quickly it is released. counting the number of planted areas alone tells us little about performance. maintenance also influences results: blocked inlets may prevent water entering a site at all. finally, a cleaner stream after construction does not prove the planting caused the change. weather, upstream activity and other improvements may have changed at the same time. comparing several sites over a longer period gives stronger evidence.

use 'i wish' and 'if only' to express wishes about the present, past, or future. the verb form after these phrases follows the same pattern as conditionals: past simple for present wishes, past perfect for past regrets, would for future wishes. 'if only' is more emphatic than 'i wish'.

use 'that' only in defining relative clauses (no commas). use 'which' in non-defining clauses (with commas). in defining clauses about things, both which and that are possible. some american editorial styles prefer that for defining clauses; british english commonly permits either. non-defining clauses about things use which, not that.

use 'which' or 'that' for objects and things, not 'who'.
use 'who' for people and 'which' for things. 'who' is the correct relative pronoun for a person.
use 'who' for people, 'which' for things, 'that' for both. arabic uses only one relative pronoun (alladhi) for all, causing this error.

use 'will' + base verb for predictions, promises, offers, spontaneous decisions, and facts about the future. 'will' does not change form (no 'he wills'). the negative is 'will not' (won't). this is the most common way to express future in english.

weak nouns in english are nouns that form their plural not by adding -s or -es, but by changing their internal vowel or adding a different suffix. these are remnants of old english declension patterns and must be memorized individually.

weak overview: “all electricity increased because the city became richer.” it invents the scope all electricity and an economic cause; coal actually falls. repair the factual pattern first, then remove the unsupported cause. read the complete model only after writing your own overview.

weak paragraph: “coaching is good. it is useful. sport is very important.” keep one claim and replace the repetition with how coaching helps a particular user. then check whether the example supports that mechanism or merely repeats the broad topic.

weak position: “both sides have advantages and i agree with everything.” revise it into a clear judgement, then keep the same judgement in the conclusion. after the fresh independent-study essay, retrieve this coverage check on a different topic; do not carry the community-project examples into it.

weak post: “both students are correct. i completely agree. there are many advantages.” it neither identifies a recommendation nor develops a new idea. keep one point of agreement and add a causal explanation plus a concrete application before increasing length.

weak post: “i agree with both classmates. their ideas are excellent. reflection is an important concept.” state your position, explain what reflection would reveal and give one concrete decision it could document. a peer reference should connect to that reasoning.

weak reflection: ‘my listening is bad.’ useful reflection: ‘i selected the speaker’s original transport plan even though but introduced a new booking.’ the useful version identifies the task, the mistaken interpretation and the evidence that changes it. it suggests a targeted action: practise distinguishing initial plans from confirmed arrangements in unfamiliar extracts.

weak response: “bags are very important today. there are advantages and disadvantages. bags are useful because they are convenient and beneficial. the environment is important. in conclusion, both views are correct.” the problem is not a shortage of impressive words. the response does not state a clear decision, develop environmental effects or add a distinct third point.

weak response: “bus passes are beneficial because they have benefits. the college should pay, although everything has disadvantages.” repair the missing causal bridge first. then identify one competing use of money and explain why the proposal should have priority or be limited. a qualification should sharpen the decision, not erase it.

weak response: “museums should be free and should charge everyone. both sides have points.” it leaves the conditions unstated. name what remains free, what may carry a charge and why the different treatment follows from the argument.

weak response: “technology is modern. all older people dislike computers. give them phones and the problem is solved.” it fails to explain adoption, stereotypes users and supplies an incomplete solution. replace the stereotype with a specific barrier, explain its mechanism and match a measure to it.

weak thesis: “both views are correct because museums are important.” more precise thesis: “permanent collections should normally be free where public funding can sustain them, while a transparent charge can be reasonable for additional exhibitions.” it states both the condition and the decision.

weak two-part answer: “language classes are good because languages are useful. more advertising is needed.” it does not explain the attendance barrier or why advertising would reach it. add a cause paragraph, then match the solution to that cause. use a full introduction and conclusion only to frame those developed answers.

weak universal claim: “any parking charge always makes travel easier.” one counterexample is a worker travelling when no alternative service runs. the example qualifies always; it does not prove that every charge fails.

wh-questions ask for specific information. they begin with a wh-word (what, where, when, why, who, whose, whom, how, etc.). the structure is: wh-word + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb. how combines with adjectives and adverbs: how much? how many? how often? how far?

when a health average hides variation an average can summarise a health outcome, but it may conceal important differences among participants. suppose a programme produces a modest average improvement while helping one group substantially and making little difference to another. reporting only the overall figure would not show who benefited or why. researchers therefore examine variation, while avoiding the temptation to explain every subgroup difference after seeing the results. dividing a small sample into many categories can produce apparent patterns by chance. a useful analysis distinguishes questions planned in advance from exploratory observations that need confirmation. the way an outcome is measured matters too. a self-reported improvement in comfort is valuable, but it is not identical to a change in physical function. neither measure should automatically replace the other. together, they may provide a fuller account of what participants experience. the writer argues for reporting benefits with enough detail to reveal uncertainty and practical meaning. this does not make an intervention ineffective simply because its effects vary. it helps readers understand which claims are supported and what further research should investigate.

when a precise term is unavailable, use a clear explanation rather than stopping for a rare synonym. listen back for a direct preference, a shared comparison dimension and a visible connection between experience and judgement. those content checks accompany, but do not replace, review of actual delivery.

when a prediction changes behaviour a station displayed predicted crowding levels to help passengers choose quieter trains. some travellers changed departure times, which meant the actual pattern differed from the prediction. the system was not necessarily defective: its information had influenced the behaviour being predicted. evaluators must therefore consider how people respond to a forecast, rather than treating every difference as a simple error.
when a question asks why a behaviour occurs and what problems it creates, causes and consequences perform separate jobs.

when a question asks why an example was mentioned, answer its explanatory role. ‘to illustrate concealment’ is a purpose; ‘because the talk concerns insects’ is only the topic. during review, connect each answer to the note level it requires and test the same distinction on the fresh recording.

when a relative clause contains a preposition, there are two styles: formal (preposition + whom/which) and informal (who/that/which + preposition at the end). in informal english, the preposition moves to the end of the clause, and the pronoun can often be omitted.

when a shortcut becomes a destination the path behind greystone station was once used mainly by commuters avoiding the main road. when a local group planted flowers along it, visitors began stopping to look rather than simply walking through. a school added labels describing insects that used the plants, and residents began recording what they saw. the project did not begin with a detailed wildlife survey. for that reason, the group cannot confidently claim that insect numbers have increased. more sightings may reflect the fact that people are now paying attention. a biology teacher has suggested recording observations at the same time each week to make future comparisons more useful. the path still needs to function as a route to the station. some large planters narrowed it too much for wheelchairs and luggage, so they were moved. volunteers also leave a clear area near the exit to prevent people stopping suddenly in front of commuters. the project’s value may lie less in a dramatic environmental result than in a changed relationship with an ordinary place. people now notice the seasons and speak with neighbours they previously passed in silence. that is a worthwhile outcome, provided enthusiasm for the garden does not undermine access for those who simply need to catch a train.

when organisations measure service quality, they often begin with satisfaction surveys. these can reveal useful experiences, but their interpretation depends on who responds. people who complete a service successfully may be more willing to answer than those who abandoned it. a high satisfaction figure can therefore coexist with serious access problems. one way to investigate this is to record where users leave a process and ask a sample of non-completers about the difficulty. the aim is not to dismiss positive feedback, but to place it alongside evidence from people whose experience is less visible. evaluators should also distinguish a polite interaction from a successful outcome. a staff member may be helpful even when the procedure prevents a person from obtaining what they need.

who benefits from a redesigned high street? a high street redesign is often presented as a choice between cars and pedestrians. that framing overlooks how many different journeys a street supports. a delivery driver, a wheelchair user, a parent with a pushchair and a shop assistant travelling home late may all need different things from the same space. the recent proposal for westbridge removes some parking to widen pavements and add seating. those changes could make the street more comfortable, especially where narrow paths currently force people to move into the road. however, the proposal says little about deliveries or access after public transport becomes less frequent in the evening. these omissions deserve attention before construction begins. this is not an argument for preserving every parking space. a street is a shared public place, and storing private vehicles should not automatically take priority over safe movement. equally, a design described as accessible should be tested with people who face practical barriers, rather than judged only from an attractive drawing. i would support a temporary trial using movable planters and marked loading areas. residents and businesses could then report specific difficulties while the layout is still easy to adjust. the council should publish what it learns, including problems that do not fit the original expectations. a successful project would improve everyday access for a wider range of people, not merely produce a more impressive photograph of the town centre.

why a pilot can be informative without being decisive a local employer tested a quieter break room after staff requested somewhere away from the main canteen. the room was used regularly, and several workers reported feeling more rested. the pilot therefore showed demand for a different kind of space. it did not establish that the room reduced sick leave. absence figures changed during the trial, but shift patterns and staffing levels also changed. a small number of cases could strongly affect the total. the evaluation separated the direct evidence of use from the more uncertain claim about health outcomes. the employer decided to retain the room while collecting longer-term feedback. this was a practical decision based on a modest cost and a clearly expressed need. it did not require pretending that every possible benefit had already been proved. the writer argues that evidence should match the scale of a decision. a low-cost reversible change may be reasonable on limited evidence, while a large permanent investment requires more. the important point is to describe the basis of the decision honestly and remain willing to adjust it.

why a tree count is not enough city planting programmes often announce how many trees will be added, because a single number is easy to communicate. that total does not show where trees will survive or whom they will benefit. a tree planted beside a pavement without enough soil may remain small, while one in a suitable site can develop a broad canopy. researchers comparing neighbourhoods therefore examine canopy cover, species diversity and maintenance as well as planting totals. they also distinguish private gardens from public streets. a leafy district may still have exposed bus stops where people wait in direct sun. the location of shade matters for access, not merely its total area. water availability creates another constraint. species chosen for rapid growth may require more care than a local maintenance team can provide. in one trial, staff recorded survival rates annually and replaced a popular but unsuitable species with a slower-growing alternative. the change reduced the headline planting target but improved the proportion of trees that established successfully. the writer argues that public reporting should connect targets with outcomes. this does not make tree planting unimportant; it makes its evaluation more useful. a modest programme with suitable sites and reliable care may create more lasting benefit than a larger announcement followed by high losses. the challenge is to communicate this complexity without making the evidence inaccessible to residents. a distributional question also arises. two districts with the same average canopy cover may offer very different experiences at street level. in one, shade may be concentrated in private gardens; in another, it may line the routes to schools and shops. a city-wide average can therefore hide whether people can reach useful shade during an ordinary journey. mapping the location of trees alongside pedestrian routes gives planners a more practical view. residents’ knowledge can improve that map. a route that looks shaded from above may still be difficult to use because roots have damaged the pavement or because there are no safe crossings. consultation does not replace measurement, but it can reveal which measurements are missing. the researchers recommend recording these observations systematically rather than treating them as isolated complaints. the same reasoning applies to future targets. announcing an ambitious number of new trees may create political support, yet a programme needs resources for the years after planting. public reports should show what was planted, what survived and which areas gained usable shade. this would make progress harder to express in one headline, but easier to connect with the reasons the programme exists.

written or partner-read rehearsal uses new wording: “the gate opens.” then “the side gate opens at noon.” then “the side gate opens at noon for visitors with tickets.” first hear a short version from a partner if available, repeat it, and compare every word. add the next phrase only when the earlier wording is retained.

written rehearsal a: “the route was longer than advertised, but the guide stopped when we needed a rest, so i would join again.” record final stance → positive with a limitation; reason → responsive guide; rejected summary → perfect route. the concession survives even though the recommendation is positive.

written rehearsal b: “the guide was friendly. nevertheless, we spent most of the day waiting, so i would choose another company.” finish stance → ___; main reason → ___; concession → ___. the friendliest adjective is not necessarily the overall judgement.

written rehearsal: a rehearsal must happen on monday and needs a keyboard. room a is free monday but has no instrument. room b has a keyboard but is free tuesday. room c is free monday if the group collects a portable keyboard. completed row for a: day yes / equipment no. complete b and c before naming a workable conditional option.

written rehearsal: “a roof over a waiting area blocks direct sunlight. this reduces heating of the seats. however, open sides do not protect users from wind.” completed mechanism → blocked sunlight. finish effect → ___; remaining condition → ___. the limitation concerns another environmental demand rather than denying the shade effect.

written rehearsal: “a standard repair costs thirty pounds. your warranty covers the inspection, but not a replacement part. we first offered monday; the confirmed appointment is wednesday.” completed slot: customer category → warranty holder. finish charge covered → ___; charge excluded → ___; appointment status → ___.

written rehearsal: “i can collect the corrected certificate after three on monday. could you confirm by noon on friday?” complete collection time → ___; reply deadline → ___. they govern different actions.

written rehearsal: “i considered cycling, but i have reserved a seat on the ferry. my sister may cycle next week.” one complete note is considered transport → cycling. finish confirmed arrangement → ___; later possibility → ___ for ___ person. attach person and time as well as the transport word.

written rehearsal: “the old café is now a meeting room; refreshments are sold beside the entrance.” complete current use of old café → ___; place to buy refreshments → ___. a historical label and a present service can occupy different places.

written rehearsal: “the walk starts at ___. bring a ___ to protect yourself if it rains.” the first gap needs a start time or starting place depending on the fuller question; the second needs a countable item. a prediction identifies a category, not a particular fact. “starts at the bridge” and “starts at nine” both fit local grammar, so read the note label.

yes/no questions are formed by inverting the subject and the auxiliary verb (do/does/did, be, have, modals). wh-questions add the question word at the beginning. subject questions such as who called? normally keep subject–verb order without adding do. embedded questions also use statement order.

yes/no questions are formed by inverting the subject and the auxiliary verb. if there's no auxiliary verb, add 'do/does/did' (which carries the tense). short answers use the auxiliary verb only: 'yes, i do.' / 'no, he doesn't.'
yes/no questions rise at the end (are you 'coming?↗). wh-questions fall (where are you 'going?↘).
yes/no questions start with the verb (to be) or do/does. wh-questions start with the question word: 'where do you live?'
yes/no questions: if/whether — he asked if i was ready.
yes/no: auxiliary + subject + main verb? | wh: wh-word + auxiliary + subject + main verb?

أصبحت وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي جزءاً لا يتجزأ من حياة الشباب، حيث تهيمن منصات مثل إنستغرام وتيك توك على روتينهم اليومي. على الجانب الإيجابي، تسمح وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي للمراهقين بالبقاء على اتصال مع الأصدقاء والعائلة واكتشاف اهتمامات جديدة والوصول إلى المحتوى التعليمي. العديد من الشباب يستخدمون المنصات لتعلم مهارات جديدة أو متابعة شخصيات ملهمة. ومع ذلك، هناك عيوب كبيرة. الاستخدام المفرط يمكن أن يؤدي إلى الإدمان والحرمان من النوم وتدني احترام الذات بسبب المقارنة الاجتماعية. التنمر الإلكتروني هو مصدر قلق خطير آخر. في رأيي، يمكن أن تكون وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي مفيدة عند استخدامها باعتدال، لكن يجب على الآباء والمدارس تثقيف الشباب حول الاستخدام المسؤول.

اقتراح: إنشاء نادٍ للتوعية البيئية مقدمة هذا الاقتراح يوصي بإنشاء نادٍ للتوعية البيئية لإشراك الطلاب في مبادرات الاستدامة. الغرض النادي سيقوم بتثقيف الطلاب حول القضايا البيئية، وتنظيم مبادرات خضراء داخل المدرسة، والمشاركة في المشاريع البيئية المحلية. الأنشطة المخطط لها - حملات إعادة تدوير شهرية ومراجعة النفايات - فعاليات زراعة الأشجار في المجتمع المحلي - محاضرات لضيوف من خبراء البيئة - حملة 'الأسبوع الأخضر' مع ورش عمل ومسابقات المستفيدون النادي سيفيد جميع الطلاب بتعزيز المسؤولية البيئية وتوفير فرص القيادة. المجتمع الأوسع سيستفيد أيضاً من مشاريعنا. الموارد المطلوبة - مشرف من قسم العلوم - لوحة إعلانات مخصصة - ميزانية أولية قدرها 200 دولار للمواد - فصل دراسي للاجتماعات الأسبوعية أعتقد أن هذا النادي سيقدم مساهمة إيجابية لمدرستنا.

اقتراح: تحسين مكتبة المدرسة مقدمة هذا الاقتراح يوصي بتحسينات عملية لجعل مكتبة المدرسة مساحة تعليمية أكثر فعالية. الوضع الحالي المكتبة غير مستغلة بشكل كافٍ. العديد من الطلاب يفضلون الدراسة في الكافتيريا لأنها أكثر راحة. الكتب قديمة وأجهزة الكمبيوتر بطيئة. التغييرات المقترحة 1. إنشاء منطقة قراءة مريحة بأكياس الفول والإضاءة الخافتة. 2. تحديث مجموعة الكتب بروايات شعبية وموارد أكاديمية. 3. استبدال أقدم 10 أجهزة كمبيوتر بأخرى جديدة. 4. إدخال نظام حجز لغرف الدراسة الجماعية. الفوائد هذه التحسينات ستزيد من استخدام المكتبة وتحسن النتائج الأكاديمية وتخلق بيئة ترحيبية لجميع الطلاب. التنفيذ يمكن تنفيذ التغييرات على مدى ثلاثة أشهر بميزانية تقارب 5,000 دولار.

بالتطلع إلى المستقبل، سيعتمد مسار حقوق الإنسان على استعداد المجتمع الدولي لمواجهة هذه التحديات المتعددة الأوجه بعزيمة متجددة. يجب الدفاع عن عالمية حقوق الإنسان ضد المحاولات الحزبية لتضييق أو تجزئة تطبيقها. كما قال الأمين العام السابق للأمم المتحدة كوفي عنان ذات مرة، حقوق الإنسان ليست رفاهية لأوقات السلام والازدهار، بل هي ضمانة أساسية تكون في أمس الحاجة إليها تحديداً عندما تكون غير مريحة لمن هم في السلطة.

بالتطلع إلى المستقبل، يبدو مستقبل الطاقة المتجددة واعداً. وضعت العديد من البلدان أهدافاً طموحة لتحقيق صافي انبعاثات كربونية صفري بحلول عام 2050. إذا أريد تحقيق هذه الأهداف، فسيلزم مزيج من الابتكار التكنولوجي والإرادة السياسية والدعم العام. على الرغم من أن التحديات لا تزال قائمة، فإن الزخم وراء الطاقة المتجددة أقوى من أي وقت مضى، وتعتبر على نطاق واسع المفتاح لمستقبل مستدام.

بالتطلع إلى المستقبل، يتحول نموذج الأمن السيبراني من وضع رد فعل يركز على السيطرة على الأضرار نحو المرونة الاستباقية. المفاهيم مثل بنية الثقة الصفرية، التي تفترض أنه لا ينبغي الوثوق بأي كيان بشكل افتراضي، تكتسب زخماً. ومع ذلك، طالما استمرت الأنظمة الرقمية في التغلغل في كل جانب من جوانب الوجود، فإن سباق التسلح بين المهاجمين والمدافعين سيستمر، مما يتطلب يقظة مستمرة وابتكاراً وثقافة قوية للوعي الأمني على كل مستوى من مستويات المجتمع.

بالتطلع نحو المستقبل، من المرجح أن تصبح نماذج التعلم المدمج التي تجمع بين التعليم عبر الإنترنت والتعليم الحضوري هي القاعدة. يهدف هذا النهج الهجين إلى الجمع بين أفضل ما في العالمين — المرونة وسهولة الوصول إلى جانب التواصل البشري والأنشطة العملية. تستثمر المؤسسات التعليمية بكثافة في البنية التحتية الرقمية لدعم هذا التحول. بينما لا يمكن للتعلم عبر الإنترنت أن يحل محل التعليم التقليدي بالكامل، فقد وسع بلا شك إمكانيات ما يمكن أن يبدو عليه التعليم في القرن الحادي والعشرين.

تشمل مشاكل الصحة النفسية الشائعة اضطرابات القلق والاكتئاب والاضطراب ثنائي القطب. تؤثر اضطرابات القلق، على سبيل المثال، على ملايين الأشخاص في جميع أنحاء العالم ويمكن أن تظهر على شكل قلق دائم أو نوبات هلع أو قلق اجتماعي. من ناحية أخرى، يتميز الاكتئاب بمشاعر مستمرة من الحزن واليأس وفقدان الاهتمام بالأنشطة التي كانت ممتعة في السابق. تتراوح هذه الحالات من خفيفة إلى شديدة وغالباً ما تتطلب تدخلاً مهنياً.

تطور دور المعلم أيضاً في سياق التعلم عبر الإنترنت. يحتاج المدرسون الآن إلى أن يكونوا بارعين في استخدام الأدوات والمنصات الرقمية، الأمر الذي يتطلب تدريباً مستمراً وتكيفاً. إن إنشاء محتوى إلكتروني جذاب يلفت انتباه الطلاب هو أكثر تحدياً بشكل كبير من إلقاء محاضرة تقليدية. على الجانب الإيجابي، توفر المنصات الرقمية للمعلمين تحليلات بيانات يمكن أن تساعدهم في تتبع تقدم الطلاب وتحديد أولئك الذين قد يحتاجون إلى دعم إضافي.

تطور علاج حالات الصحة النفسية بشكل كبير على مر السنين. أثبت العلاج، مثل العلاج السلوكي المعرفي، فعاليته العالية للعديد من الأفراد. يمكن أيضاً وصف الأدوية للمساعدة في إدارة الأعراض، خاصة في الحالات الأكثر شدة. علاوة على ذلك، ثبت أن تغييرات نمط الحياة بما في ذلك ممارسة الرياضة بانتظام واتباع نظام غذائي متوازن والنوم الكافي تحسن السلامة النفسية بشكل كبير.

تظهر هذه الصورة الفوتوغرافية سوق شارع مزدحماً فيما يبدو أنها مدينة قديمة. في المقدمة، هناك عدة أكشاك تبيع الفواكه والخضروات الطازجة. بائع يرتدي مئزراً أزرق يخدم زبونة تفحص المنتجات بعناية. على اليسار، زبائن آخرون ينتظرون ويتحدثون مع بعضهم البعض. في الخلفية، أستطيع رؤية مبانٍ قديمة وبرج كنيسة. يبدو المكان كمركز مدينة تاريخي، ربما في أوروبا. الطقس مشمس والألوان دافئة وجذابة — الكثير من الأحمر والأخضر والبرتقالي من الفاكهة. الأجواء تبدو حيوية ومبهجة. الناس يبدون مسترخين وودودين. لدي انطباع بأن هذا مشهد صباحي معتاد حيث يقوم السكان المحليون بتسوقهم اليومي. أعتقد أن هذه الصورة تلتقط جوهر الأسواق التقليدية في الشارع. إنها تظهر الحياة المجتمعية وأهمية الطعام الطازج المحلي. شخصياً، تروقني هذه الصورة لأنني أستمتع بالتسوق في الأسواق وتجربة الأجواء النابضة بالحياة.

تقرير: تقييم دورة اللغة الإنجليزية مقدمة هذا التقرير يقيم دورة اللغة الإنجليزية المكثفة لمدة 4 أسابيع التي حضرتها في أكاديمية اللغة العالمية من 5 مايو إلى 30 مايو. محتوى الدورة غطت الدورة المهارات الأربع: القراءة والكتابة والتحدث والاستماع. المواد كانت حديثة وذات صلة باحتياجاتي. شرح القواعد كان واضحاً بشكل خاص. جودة التدريس المعلمون كانوا ذوي خبرة ومتحمسين. أحجام الفصول كانت صغيرة، مما سمح باهتمام فردي. التغذية الراجعة على الأعمال الكتابية كانت مفصلة ومفيدة. المرافق الفصول الدراسية مجهزة تجهيزاً جيداً بسبورات بيضاء تفاعلية. ومع ذلك، كان اتصال wifi غير موثوق في بعض الأحيان. التوصية أوصي بمواصلة هذه الدورة للمتعلمين في المستوى المتوسط. التحسين الوحيد سيكون ترقية خدمة wifi.

تقرير: مراجعة مرافق المدرسة مقدمة الغرض من هذا التقرير هو تقييم الوضع الحالي لمرافق المدرسة واقتراح التحسينات. النتائج المكتبة مجهزة جيداً بالكتب وأجهزة الكمبيوتر، لكن العديد من أجهزة الكمبيوتر قديمة وبطيئة. المرافق الرياضية، بما في ذلك ملعب كرة القدم وملعب كرة السلة، في حالة جيدة. ومع ذلك، تحتاج غرف تغيير الملابس إلى تجديد. الكافتيريا تقدم قائمة محدودة وقد أبلغ الطلاب أنه لا توجد مساحات جلوس كافية خلال وقت الغداء. التوصيات 1. ترقية أجهزة الكمبيوتر في المكتبة بمعدات حديثة. 2. تجديد غرف تغيير الملابس بخزائن ودشات جديدة. 3. توسيع منطقة جلوس الكافتيريا. آمل أن يتم النظر في هذه التوصيات.

تقرير: نتائج استبيان رضا الطلاب مقدمة هذا التقرير يعرض نتائج استبيان أجري بين 200 طالب حول رضاهم عن الحياة الجامعية. جودة التدريس 85% من الطلاب قيموا جودة التدريس بأنها جيدة أو ممتازة. الشاغل الرئيسي كان نقص جلسات المراجعة قبل الامتحانات. المرافق المكتبة تلقت ردود فعل إيجابية بنسبة رضا 78%. ومع ذلك، معمل الكمبيوتر حصل على تقييم ضعيف بنسبة رضا 45% فقط بسبب البرامج القديمة. الأنشطة الاجتماعية فقط 40% من الطلاب كانوا راضين عن الأنشطة الاجتماعية المقدمة. طلب الكثيرون المزيد من الأندية الرياضية والفعاليات الثقافية. التوصيات 1. إدخال جلسات مراجعة أسبوعية قبل الامتحانات. 2. تحديث برامج معمل الكمبيوتر. 3. إنشاء أندية رياضية وجمعيات ثقافية جديدة.

شهد القرن العشرون لحظة فاصلة في إضفاء الطابع المؤسسي على حقوق الإنسان. حشدت فظائع الحربين العالميتين المجتمع الدولي لوضع معيار عالمي للحماية. في عام 1948، اعتمدت الجمعية العامة للأمم المتحدة الإعلان العالمي لحقوق الإنسان، وهي وثيقة تاريخية كرست الحقوق المدنية والسياسية والاقتصادية والاجتماعية والثقافية باعتبارها غير قابلة للتجزئة ومترابطة. وضع هذا الإعلان حجر الزاوية للنظام الدولي الحديث لحقوق الإنسان.

شهدت الطاقة الشمسية بشكل خاص نمواً ملحوظاً على مدى العقد الماضي. أصبح إنتاج الألواح الكهروضوئية أقل تكلفة بشكل كبير، وتحسنت كفاءتها بشكل هائل. يقوم العديد من الأسر الآن بتركيب ألواح شمسية على أسطح منازلهم، مما يسمح لهم بتوليد الكهرباء الخاصة بهم وحتى بيع الفائض منها إلى الشبكة العامة. تم تشجيع هذا الاتجاه من خلال الدعم الحكومي والحوافز الضريبية في العديد من البلدان.

مسألة ما إذا كان يجب على الطلاب العمل بوظائف بدوام جزئي هي موضوع نقاش واسع. من ناحية، العمل بدوام جزئي يقدم فوائد عديدة. يكتسب الطلاب الاستقلال المالي، ويتعلمون مهارات إدارة الوقت القيمة، ويكتسبون خبرة عملية تبدو مثيرة للإعجاب في سيرهم الذاتية. وظائف مثل التدريس الخصوصي أو العمل في متجر أو خدمة المطاعم تعلم المسؤولية ومهارات التواصل. من ناحية أخرى، يمكن أن يؤثر العمل سلباً على الأداء الأكاديمي إذا لم يدير الطلاب وقتهم بشكل جيد. قد تؤدي ساعات العمل الطويلة إلى الإرهاق وتقليل الوقت للواجبات المنزلية أو المراجعة. في رأيي، العمل بدوام جزئي مفيد طالما لا يتجاوز 10-15 ساعة أسبوعياً ولا يتعارض مع الدراسة.

مع be: الفاعل ثم be ثم not. ومع الفعل الناقص: الفاعل ثم الفعل الناقص ثم not. ومع الأفعال الأخرى: do أو does أو did ثم not ثم أصل الفعل. تسبق no الاسم مثل no money، بينما تنفي not الفعل أو الوصف مثل not happy.
