‘...but i doubt it will survive heavy use.’

‘a company sources components from several countries’ describes where inputs come from. ‘it outsources a service’ describes transferring that work to another provider, which need not always be overseas. ‘it relocates production’ describes a change in where production occurs. similar business topics do not make these expressions identical.
‘a few participants reported improvement’ can become ‘improvement was reported by a small number of participants.’
‘a later deadline may help commuters, but a short check-in beforehand could reveal problems early enough for staff to respond.’
‘a picnic would be inexpensive. if the weather changes, though, would the school hall be a better backup?’
‘a shared printer would help pupils without one at home because they could prepare paper copies before class.’

‘a useful improvement in access’ cannot become ‘a perfect solution for all residents’. the stronger option adds universality and removes limitations. ‘not the only measure’ cannot become ‘completely irrelevant’: an author can oppose exclusive reliance on publicity while accepting it as one source of information.
‘although demand increased, the lack of a comparison site makes the campaign’s contribution uncertain.’

‘although the gallery is closed, the upstairs exhibition remains open’ contrasts two facilities. because would change the relationship to cause. retain the conjunction as part of the meaning group instead of memorising only gallery, closed and open.
‘although the route is shorter, the steep climb makes it slower for some cyclists.’

‘analysis continues now’ describes an ongoing situation. ‘researchers have analysed three samples so far’ counts results up to now. ‘they analysed three samples in september 2024’ places completed work in a finished period. since does not automatically require a progressive: ‘the centre has opened on saturdays since 2022’ can describe a repeated schedule.

‘attendance increased by 60’ uses a verb. ‘there was an increase of 60 in attendance’ uses a noun. do not mix them as ‘there was an increased by 60’. a noun can take an adjective: a gradual increase. a verb can take an adverb: increased gradually. choose the frame first, then its modifier.

‘borrowers can always keep equipment longer if they email’ is unsupported. it drops both the deadline and the competing-booking condition. practical comprehension often depends on retaining such small restrictions.
‘both activities need concentration, but the chess players may spend more time planning whereas the dancers have to react while moving.’

‘bring identification’ requires the item. ‘a jacket will be provided’ describes a supplied item. ‘do not bring safety clothing’ is a prohibition or instruction against bringing it, not a statement that clothing is unnecessary in every situation. an exception such as unless you have already completed induction narrows the group that must act.
‘by the garden / i can relax between chapters’ groups related information.
‘car restrictions are reasonable in crowded shopping streets if reliable access remains for deliveries and people with mobility needs.’

‘colour can warn predators’ reports a possible function. ‘colour always prevents attacks’ makes a universal claim. the difference concerns meaning, not stylistic variety. a final limitation—behaviour and habitat also matter—often explains why one feature cannot classify every case.
‘could you arrange a replacement?’ / ‘could you bring the spare?’

‘could you explain when the course begins?’ has a courteous main question plus the embedded clause when the course begins. inside it, subject precedes verb. compare the direct ‘when does the course begin?’ the meaning stays about time, but the clause’s grammatical role changes.
‘could you lower the blinds?’ asks for an action.
‘could you lower the blinds?’ → ‘of course; the sunlight is quite strong.’
‘could you send a copy so i can register before monday?’
‘could you send the second ticket before friday?’
‘critics call the scheme wasteful; the author argues that its improved access justifies the cost.’

‘draw a conclusion from the findings’ identifies an inference, while ‘collect data’ identifies the material used to investigate. a conclusion is not the same as raw data. keeping these roles separate helps both reading and argument writing: describe what was measured before evaluating what follows.

‘each student has a badge’ treats the members individually with singular student. ‘all students have badges’ uses a plural subject. ‘one of the students has a badge’ has one as the head; of the students identifies the group. ‘a number of students have registered’ is a conventional plural pattern, whereas ‘the number of students has increased’ describes a singular total.

‘every fountain will work when a walker arrives’ exceeds the source. ‘the organisers reject all public reports’ reverses their checking process. ‘the map provides no help’ discards the useful-assistance judgement. a supported summary retains both practical value and limits.
‘every user failed’ does not follow from several needing help.
‘everything included’ supplies no additional materials fee to calculate.
‘flexible hours are useful when teams share a short overlap period, because coordination can continue while individuals adjust their start times.’
‘guests need a pass except during the public tour from two to three.’
‘having checked the address, noor sent the parcel.’

‘how do i reserve the booth?’ suggests an intention to arrange it, not an existing reservation. ‘i have reserved it’ establishes a completed action. ‘could i reserve it?’ requests permission or availability. the verb form and conversational stage determine which conclusion is safe.
‘i can read on the way to college.’
‘i decided i could help’ expresses willingness after reluctance.
‘i expected the course to be easy. the first task was hard, but the feedback helped me improve.’ summarise the development.
‘i prefer a weekly plan because it leaves room for changes. on busy days, i can move a reading session to the following morning.’
‘i prefer the early train because it is usually less crowded. i can read on the way to college.’
‘i said the first session, not the last one.’
‘i used to revise late, but now i work earlier because i concentrate better.’ → ‘i have changed from late revision to earlier sessions that suit my concentration.’
‘i was exhausted by the end, but the practical experience was worth the effort.’ is the overall evaluation necessarily negative?

‘i was nervous before the first session, but the tutor made it manageable’ reports an initial feeling followed by a positive experience. choosing a negative evaluation because nervous was heard ignores the development. ‘the idea is attractive, although staffing is unresolved’ supports interest with a practical reservation.
‘if a place becomes available, you can join the seminar.’

‘if places remain, students may register online’ makes permission conditional on availability. it does not promise available places. ‘if more places became available, i would register’ imagines a less certain situation. the forms express different viewpoints; not every conditional is a fixed prediction.
‘individual reflection may reveal what each student learned, especially when a group divides the work unevenly.’
‘initially i avoided the project. once i saw the small tasks available, i decided i could help.’
‘it closes at six on sundays’ is false because sunday is not mentioned.

‘it is unnecessary to book’ becomes ‘you do not have to book.’ do not replace it with must not book: lack of necessity permits booking, while prohibition forbids it. a preference changes pattern too: ‘i prefer walking to driving’ → ‘i would rather walk than drive.’ rather takes a base verb here, not walking. the new clause must preserve which option is preferred.
‘it sounds worthwhile, provided we can arrange cover for the evening staff.’
‘larger windows reduced lighting costs. in the west-facing rooms, however, cooling demand increased.’

‘learning with others’ can become ‘practising in a small group’ when the context supports it. it cannot automatically become teaching a class, because the participant’s role changes. ‘explain your preference and describe an experience’ requires both judgement and evidence. restating only the topic leaves a demand unanswered.

‘less heat escaped after shutters were installed’ can restate ‘heat loss decreased following installation of shutters.’ both preserve the direction of change and the affected process. ‘the shutters created more heat’ changes reduced loss into production. a dictionary synonym for one word cannot protect the meaning of the whole claim.
‘lockers are available to enrolled students. keys must be returned by six.’
‘looking for a quiet study space?’ introduces that angle.
‘looking for somewhere to study between classes? the community centre has desks beside the courtyard.’
‘makes the building more ___’ needs an adjective here.

‘members may enter after induction. visitors must be accompanied. equipment is available except during maintenance.’ these clauses govern different groups and resources. membership alone does not remove the induction condition; visitor access requires accompaniment; equipment permission changes during maintenance. a positive general phrase cannot cancel a specific restriction.
‘my lab session overlaps with the briefing. would attending the afternoon briefing be possible? please let me know whether i should register again.’
‘my receipt lists two tickets, but the attachment contains one. could you send the second ticket before friday?’
‘nora offered to lead the session. ___ . her replacement arrived at noon.’ what information must a plausible middle sentence establish?

‘not only did the change reduce delays, but it also improved access’ uses inversion in the fronted first clause. the second clause retains its ordinary statement frame. ‘only after the inspection did staff reopen the room’ places the time restriction first; the reopening follows the inspection. moving only can change what is restricted, so check the intended focus.
‘of course’ accepts the request without repeating the question.

‘participation rose after the timetable changed’ reports sequence. ‘the timetable change caused the rise’ needs stronger evidence about alternative explanations. if only before/after counts are supplied, use cautious association language. a grammatical sentence can still make an unsupported claim.
‘people may resist a new system when the familiar one lets them predict what will happen, even if the new system has advantages.’
‘place the folders beside the main entrance.’

‘please close the door’ can introduce door for the first time because the room makes the intended door identifiable. ‘the sun’ commonly names a unique referent in everyday context. ‘the manager’ may be identifiable inside a particular workplace even if no earlier sentence introduced a manager. first mention therefore does not automatically require a.
‘put my name down for that’ accepts the thursday place.
‘rarely had the team faced such a delay.’ / ‘it was the missing permit that caused the delay.’
‘reopening month: ___’ can take june, not a guessed repair price.

‘researchers observe behaviour’ uses a verb; ‘the observation was useful’ uses a noun; ‘an observational study’ uses an adjective. ‘a clear observe’ fails because the noun phrase needs a noun head. ‘the finding suggests that...’ uses a clause complement, while ‘a suggestion about practice’ uses a noun phrase.
‘reserve the larger room’ confirms the choice.
‘room twelve was booked, so meet in room twenty instead.’ which room should you enter?
‘shared gardens can encourage contact because neighbours have a reason to talk while caring for the same space.’

‘some residents call the scheme a complete success, but the author recommends waiting for winter data’ contains two views. complete success belongs to residents; cautious delay belongs to the author. a question about the writer cannot be answered by copying the first quoted opinion.
‘staff may choose either shift, but everyone must complete the safety briefing.’

‘students who completed induction may enter’ restricts permission. removing who completed induction widens the rule. ‘they must collect a badge’ needs a clear referent for they; if staff and students were both mentioned, repeat the noun when necessary.

‘the assistant explained why the procedure had changed’ contains a main clause and an embedded explanation. inside why, use statement order: the procedure had changed. ‘why had the procedure changed?’ is a direct question and has a different frame.
‘the assistant labelled the bottles before noon.’ → ‘the bottles were labelled by the assistant before noon.’
‘the beans are roasted’ foregrounds the material being processed.
‘the book is on loan.’ ‘could i reserve it?’ ‘certainly, i will add your name.’ what is agreed?
‘the bridge reopened in june after repairs.’ this gives a date, a change of state and a sequence, but no repair cost.
‘the bridge reopened in june’ supplies a reopening month.
‘the chart shows enrolment. numbers rose in 2018; the dotted line projects a further rise in 2030.’

‘the chart shows’ describes the visual in front of the reader now. ‘visits fell in 2020’ describes a completed observation. the two present/past forms can coexist correctly in the same sentence: ‘the chart shows that visits fell in 2020.’ consistency means matching each verb to its job, not forcing every verb into the same tense.
‘the clinic proposed longer hours. the council rejected the proposal because staffing funds were unavailable.’
‘the coating reduced damage only when the surface was dry.’ note: the coating worked on a ___ surface.
‘the coating worked on a ___ surface’ → dry.

‘the council discussed the app with the library, but it was unavailable’ leaves it unclear whether the app or library was unavailable. ‘the app was unavailable’ resolves the referent. ‘this problem’ can summarise an earlier proposition, but name the problem when several possibilities compete.
‘the design is attractive, although i’m not convinced it will survive heavy use.’
‘the desk opens at nine; collections begin at ten.’ which time answers a collection question?

‘the equipment was delivered’ uses singular agreement with the uncountable head. ‘the three items of equipment were delivered’ has plural items as its head. the number of physical objects does not directly determine the grammar of equipment.
‘the exhibition closes early today. please collect your bags before four.’ state the purpose.
‘the field-trip form will not open on my account. could you send an accessible copy so i can register before monday?’
‘the filter worked well unless the water contained oil.’ state the exception in a short note.
‘the first friendly question helped break the ice.’

‘the guide will meet visitors near the information desk’ can be retained as subject → action → people → location. this organisation reduces the burden of remembering an unstructured sound sequence. however, reconstructing the idea as ‘a guide meets people by a desk’ changes articles, tense and nouns. similar meaning is not accurate repetition.
‘the hall might be free on monday. we have not checked yet.’ is monday a confirmed booking?
‘the help desk is open all afternoon. after two, visitors need an appointment.’ a walk-in arrives at three.

‘the library had opened many years earlier’ mentions the eventual venue but does not explain a move. ‘the exhibition was cancelled’ conflicts with visitors praising it. ‘every picture was displayed’ conflicts with selecting two. test the whole reconstructed account, not just the nouns either side of the gap.

‘the list of rooms is on the wall’ has singular list as its subject head. rooms is inside a modifying phrase. compare ‘the rooms on the list are available’, where rooms is the plural head. find the complete subject, then temporarily remove the modifier to test the basic clause: the list is; the rooms are.
‘the list of workshop dates is on the wall.’ / ‘the lists of workshop dates are on the wall.’
‘the pilot suggests that the reminder may improve attendance among these volunteers.’
‘the players may need more time to plan’ marks an inference.

‘the policy may reduce delays’ leaves uncertainty and allows remaining delays. ‘the policy will eradicate every inconvenience’ strengthens certainty, completeness and scope. a vocabulary substitution that changes any of these alters the claim. before choosing a verb, ask what the evidence actually supports: suggests, indicates, demonstrates and proves are not interchangeable in every context.

‘the project was successful’ uses an adjective complement after was. ‘the team completed it successfully’ uses an adverb modifying completed. ‘its success depended on volunteers’ uses a noun as subject. read the clause to identify which job is required before choosing the familiar-looking form.

‘the proposal, which residents developed after several meetings, was revised when a safety inspection identified a problem’ has main subject proposal and main verb was revised. the relative clause supplies background authorship; the when-clause supplies the trigger. reducing it to residents identified a problem changes who performed the inspection.
‘the proposal’ refers to the clinic’s plan for longer hours.
‘the question helped everyone relax’ can express the idea plainly.
‘the questionnaire indicates a preference among respondents; it does not measure their later purchases.’
‘the reading corner faces the garden, so i can rest my eyes between chapters without leaving my seat.’
‘the red seats cost less, but i need an aisle seat, so i will take the blue one.’ which colour is chosen?

‘the results suggest a possible association’ is cautious. ‘the results prove the mechanism universally’ needs much stronger support. ‘a representative sample’ describes coverage of a population; it should not be claimed merely because a study has many participants. a large but narrow group can still leave important people out.

‘the revised procedure reduces delays’ has subject the revised procedure, finite verb reduces and object delays. revised is a modifier inside the subject phrase; it does not replace the main verb. in ‘additional evidence becomes available’, becomes links evidence to the adjective available rather than taking a direct object.
‘the revised rule allow...’ has a singular-subject agreement error.
‘the riverside entrance is flooded. visitors should use the west gate today.’
‘the service is reliable’ describes dependable performance. ‘the service is frequent’ describes how often it runs.
‘the shaded sites retained more moisture, although soil depth also differed. tree cover may have contributed.’

‘the shop closes at six, but the collection desk closes at four’ contains two true deadlines. for collection, four is the relevant one. six is not necessarily a false detail; it belongs to a different service. a workplace induction may similarly distinguish an arrival time, starting time and time when equipment is available.
‘the small menu suits a quick lunch.’
‘the small room is cheaper, but we need the projector, so please reserve the larger one.’
‘the start time is still ten’ preserves the time.

‘the studio used to be the exhibition room, but exhibitions now take place upstairs’ supplies history and current function. a present-day plan needs studio in the old room, not exhibition. a facility-matching question might instead ask which space stays open late; its answer depends on a feature, not a direction.
‘the talk is in hall b—actually, hall d. the start time is still ten.’

‘the team made steady progress after agreeing clear roles. one volunteer took responsibility for safety, while another offered advice to visitors. the first event was successful, although finding replacement parts remained difficult.’ made progress describes advancement; took responsibility names ownership of a task; offered advice describes help; successful evaluates the event without claiming every problem disappeared.
‘the team replaced the paper tickets with an app. this change reduced printing costs.’

‘the trial suggests a possible benefit’ offers tentative support. ‘the trial proves a benefit for every learner’ raises certainty and widens scope. even if proves is familiar academic vocabulary, it is unsuitable when the source keeps the result provisional. ‘consistent with’ means compatible with an earlier finding, not necessarily caused by it or identical in every respect.

‘the trial that involved three neighbourhoods was short’ has singular trial as the main subject; neighbourhoods belongs inside the relative clause. ‘the residents who attended were satisfied’ has plural residents. read each verb with its own subject rather than the nearest noun.
‘the trial, which involved two schools, was small, although its findings justified further investigation.’
‘the workshop is now online; your original booking remains valid.’ what action and non-action follow?
‘the workshop that includes field visits prepares students for independent research.’
‘the workshop was demanding, but i would gladly attend another.’ is the final attitude negative? explain.
‘the workshop will meet online tomorrow. the ten o’clock start and the preparation task remain the same.’
‘the £70 estimate excluded materials. we chose the £95 offer with everything included.’
‘they called off the trip’ means they cancelled it. ‘they put off the trip’ means they postponed it.
‘they reached an agreement.’ / ‘they agreed on a date.’
‘this change reduced printing costs’ follows the switch to an app.
‘this change’ can refer to replacing paper tickets.

‘this could help students explain their decisions’ is suitable academic language. replacing it with ‘this pedagogical paradigm will eradicate all opacity’ makes the claim less natural and much stronger. formality does not require avoiding help, people or problem whenever they are the clearest words.

‘three studies supplied useful information’ distinguishes countable investigations from the material they produced. ‘much research’ and ‘many studies’ use different quantifiers. to count advice, use suggestions or pieces of advice. to count equipment, name the items or use items of equipment.
‘use the west gate today’ redirects visitors.

‘visitors who arrive after the tour begins should wait near reception’ contains a main instruction and a clause identifying late arrivals. repeating only ‘visitors should wait near reception’ broadens the rule to everyone. replacing after with before reverses who the instruction concerns.
‘visitors who need a parking permit should contact reception after nine.’

‘walking to the station, maya noticed the new sign’ means maya was walking and maya noticed. ‘walking to the station, the rain began’ wrongly suggests the rain was walking. repair it with a full clause when subjects differ: ‘while maya was walking to the station, the rain began.’ shortening is useful only when it preserves a clear relationship.
‘we considered tuesday, but confirmed thursday at eleven.’ what date and time should your note retain?
‘we might use room b. i will ask tomorrow.’ is room b confirmed?
‘we received useful feedback from four reviewers’ / ‘we received four detailed comments.’
‘we rented a cottage. the kitchen overlooked fields.’
‘we tested a paper form and an online form. ___ it also reduced postage.’ write a bridging sentence.

‘we visited a museum on saturday. the museum had a small garden. we sat in the garden and discussed art. the art in the entrance hall was created by local students.’ a introduces the museum; the then identifies it. a introduces the garden; the next sentence refers back to it. art names a general topic with no article; the art in the entrance hall identifies a specific collection.

‘we were on the same page’ can mean we shared an understanding. it is unsuitable if the people merely occupied the same room but disagreed about the plan. ‘i weighed the pros and cons’ describes considering benefits and drawbacks; it needs an actual decision context. inserting either phrase into every answer can make the message less natural.

‘when does registration close?’ is a direct question: does carries present tense and close stays base. ‘please explain when registration closes’ embeds that information question with statement order. ‘could you explain whether registration remains open?’ asks about an unresolved yes/no condition using whether.
‘where does the seminar take place?’ / ‘could you tell me where the seminar takes place?’

‘why did you start?’ asks for an initial reason. ‘what matters most now?’ asks for a current evaluation. ‘what would you change next time?’ asks for a future revision based on experience. a detail that correctly answers one can be a distractor for another.

‘would it be possible to attend another induction?’ uses a modal frame plus an infinitive. ‘could you confirm whether another session is available?’ embeds a statement-order clause. neither needs repeated apologies to be respectful. ‘we will meet at two’ wrongly treats the suggested alternative as agreed.
‘would the school hall be a useful backup?’
‘would you mind sending the schedule?’ why is ‘not at all—i will email it’ a relevant response?
‘you need not print the form, but you must sign it.’ is printing forbidden?
“a park, because i can walk there after work and relax.”
“a short reflection can help students explain a decision” is clear and appropriately qualified. the other options assert a false language rule or use inflated wording.

“a small number of participants said they had improved” preserves the limited group and reported result. “the treatment improved everyone” changes scope and adds a causal claim. the photograph supplies equipment vocabulary, not evidence for either research statement.
“according to” can introduce the noun phrase “the study’s results”; no grammatical ban applies.

“adapting an outdoor seating area” connects the expansion, the weather problem and the response. “the number of tables” is too narrow. a main idea explains how the details fit together rather than naming one visible object.

“although evening classes widen access, some adults still need childcare in order to attend.” the concession accepts a benefit but limits its reach. “adults who work during the day may benefit from evening sessions” uses an identifying relative clause. “because they work during the day” alone is a fragment in this context; it needs a main clause.

“an otherwise empty period.” the cinema used time that was not already serving another screening. the passage does not say prices increased or staff worked unpaid. those are imaginable explanations, not supplied facts.
“attendance fell at first, then recovered after the timetable changed.” the project had an early difficulty, not a permanent decline.

“attendance rose by 60 to 260 in 2023, before falling slightly to 250 in 2024.” alternative noun form: “there was an increase of 60 in attendance in 2023.” a separate comparison is “the 2024 figure was 50 higher than in 2022.”

“because the signs were unclear, we asked at reception.” a reason clause alone leaves the main assertion unfinished. for the second pair, “although the guide arrived, we could not enter” accepts arrival while reporting an unexpected restriction; use because only if arrival actually caused it.

“could you arrange a replacement key?” suits an administrative request. “could you bring me the spare key?” can suit a friend. develop the necessary circumstances for the actual reader; adding elaborate vocabulary without clarifying the action does not improve the message.

“could you clarify the collection time?” seeks information. “i wish to make a formal complaint” performs a stronger action that must match the intended purpose. do not escalate a request just to display vocabulary.

“could you explain why the gate is locked?” subject the gate precedes is inside the embedded clause. for the fresh conversion, check both the outer request and the inner proposition separately. after another module, retrieve the difference without copying the shop or gate wording.

“could you explain why these results differ?” begins with a polite main-clause question and embeds “why these results differ” in statement order. “the slides include several useful examples.” agrees with the plural subject slides. both sentences serve the presentation-advice context.

“could you send the missing ticket before friday?” follows a brief statement of the two-ticket purchase and one-ticket delivery. the recipient can identify the problem and requested response. an invented reference number would add unsupported information.
“could you tell me where the class meets? i need to check whether i can arrive after work.” the embedded clause uses subject–verb order. the reason explains the practical need without a long apology.

“could you tell me where the seminar takes place?” uses statement order inside the embedded clause. does is removed from that clause and the singular ending returns in takes. the image does not provide an actual seminar location.
“damaged during the storm, the sign was replaced” describes the sign as affected. before choosing an -ing or participle form, name whether the subject does or receives the action.

“despite the rain, the pedestrians continued walking.” although introduces the clause it was raining; despite takes the noun phrase the rain. both versions retain the concession. the photograph supplies a scene, not evidence about anyone’s intentions.
“do not use my laptop,” ana said. told → ana ___ use her laptop.
“enrolled students may borrow a locker key; it must be returned by six.” does student status remove the return deadline?

“every volunteer used the cup daily” → false: only twelve of forty did so. “the reusable cups were cheaper than disposable cups” → not given: no cost comparison is supplied. “the author considers publicity more important than convenience” → no: the writer explicitly ranks convenience higher.

“had already begun.” the beginning precedes her arrival. “began when she arrived” locates the beginning at that arrival instead. the choice changes the account; it is not a matter of making the sentence sound more advanced.

“have written” counts completed pages. “have been working” naturally emphasises the continuing activity and its present consequence. it is not the only grammatical way to describe that history; explain the intended meaning rather than invent a universal ban on simple forms.
“having locked the gate, the volunteers returned the key.” keep the full after-clause when actors differ or the reduced phrase would be ambiguous. shorter is not automatically better.
“i avoided the project at first. once we divided it into smaller jobs, i wanted to help.” what changed, and what explains it?

“i formerly studied late in the day; now i prefer an earlier session because i concentrate better then.” preserves the change and its reason. it does not claim that late study is impossible or that the preference applies to everyone.
“i joined for the qualification, but the practical experience mattered more.” → the value changed from the initial expectation.
“i missed two contrast questions because i selected the first idea.” → replay a fresh extract and note the final judgement.
“i use a timetable.” with no reason
“i wanted to book friday, but it was full, so i chose saturday.” → the booking is for saturday.
“i work on tuesday.” “there is a thursday place.” “please put my name down for that.” which day is accepted?

“if a place becomes available, you can join the workshop.” joining is possible under the stated condition. the sentence neither guarantees a vacancy nor grants an unconditional place. the published blank planner records no actual booking availability.
“it used to cost twenty; the new price is twenty-five.” → current price: twenty-five.
“it was expensive, but i would happily go again.” → the overall recommendation is positive.

“it was the label that rina corrected yesterday.” keep the actor, object and time. after the live transformations, retrieve a new ordinary clause and decide whether emphasis is useful before fronting it.

“it would suit patient beginners who enjoy solving practical problems, provided they follow the volunteer’s safety advice.” it identifies readers and a meaningful condition. a different audience is valid if the preceding experience supports it.
“last year—actually, two years ago—i studied there.”
“may help” preserves the passage’s qualified possible effect.

“members who completed the safety briefing.” by members alone removes the safety restriction. in the fresh live sentences, preserve eligibility, time and reference before deciding whether the passive is preferable. return later with a new instruction and explain what changes if its relative clause is deleted.

“my lab overlaps with the morning briefing. could i join the afternoon session instead? should i register again?” gives each sentence a different communication job. the blank planner is a context image, not a record of these invented appointments.
“my town is very nice” → “on saturday mornings the old market becomes a place to hear local musicians and try food from nearby farms.”

“of course; i will do that” accepts the request. a response only explaining what blinds are would miss the communicative action. the pictured people are not the speakers of this invented exchange; the scene supplies a context for the language.
“put off” means postpone. the two-word answer keeps put unchanged. “put away” is grammatical but changes the meaning.
“requests fell by 16 to 64”; “there was a fall of 16 in requests.” the relative fall is 16/80 = 20%. sixteen is the change, not the ending value.

“rina corrected the label yesterday.” for who, use “it was rina who corrected the label.” for when, use “it was yesterday that rina corrected the label.” partly complete a cleft focusing the object, then compare what the listener notices.
“roadworks moved collection from the station to the hall.” answer why, where now and where before separately.
“staff may choose either shift. everyone must attend the briefing.” which part is optional and which is compulsory?
“still begin at 2 pm” explicitly preserves the start time.
“students pay nine” identifies the category-specific fee.

“suggests” here means provides tentative support for, not conclusively proves. “persists” means continues over time. a faithful summary is “the initial evidence is compatible with a benefit, but its longer-term reach remains to be investigated.”

“that could keep the cost down. if the weather changes, could we use a hall instead?” keeps the partner’s reason, adds a relevant condition and invites a shared decision. it does not abandon the discussion for an unrelated prepared speech.
“that should work” follows the booth proposal, and the student asks how to reserve it.
“the archive is small, but collecting a few accounts carefully matters more to me than expanding quickly.” is rapid expansion the priority?

“the caretaker checked the lights last night.” “the caretaker did not check the lights last night.” last night places this event in a finished past period. “has checked” would create a present-perfect frame that conflicts with that explicit event time in ordinary use.

“the coach suggested practising slowly” uses an -ing action after suggested. “the coach recommended that we practise slowly” uses a that-clause. both are possible constructions; do not invent a ban on every form except -ing. complete “the librarian recommended ___ the catalogue first (check).”
“the coating reduced damage, but only when the surface was dry.” complete “effective on a ___ surface” and explain why reduced damage alone is incomplete.
“the earlier offer was £70 excluding materials. we selected the £95 all-inclusive offer.” what cost is supported, and what must not be added?

“the equipment was delivered on monday” uses singular agreement with uncountable equipment. “three microscopes were delivered” uses plural agreement with a countable head. “two studies provided useful information” distinguishes investigations from what they produced.
“the first session is free; later sessions cost eight pounds.” → the introductory session costs nothing.
“the history of all cities began long ago.”

“the participation rate increased by 15 percentage points, from 30% to 45%.” “the number of participants increased by 300, from 600 to 900.” both relative changes are 50%, but they describe different measures. “according to the programme’s results, participation increased” is a grammatical attribution.

“the pass covers both the exhibition and the workshop” joins two noun phrases. “the pass covers both visiting the exhibition and attending the workshop” joins two -ing phrases. complete “the guide explained both ___ and ___” with matching types before trying mixed supplied tokens.

“the pilot suggests a possible attendance benefit for this group” preserves preliminary evidence, possibility and a limited population. proves, everyone and always would strengthen or widen the claim. the equipment photograph is not evidence of the reminder’s effectiveness.

“the questionnaire indicates a preference for option a among respondents” retains the measured response and sample. predicting everyone’s later purchases changes both the outcome and the population. the equipment photograph supplies no questionnaire data or behavioural forecast.

“the reading link will not open, so i cannot prepare the comparison. could you send an accessible copy before thursday’s seminar?” links circumstance, consequence and requested help. a polite opening alone would not make the message actionable.

“the revised procedure reduces unnecessary delays.” uses singular reduces with procedure and plural delays as its object. “each record includes a clear description.” needs the noun description after the article and adjective. “additional evidence becomes available after testing.” uses an adjective complement after becomes.

“the revised rule allows visitors to book ahead.” the singular subject rule requires allows. the repair adds no date, guarantee, price or claim that every visitor will book. a narrow correction can be sufficient when the rest of the message is clear.

“the samples were labelled by the assistant.” samples becomes the grammatical subject; were labelled preserves the completed past event. the actor remains in by the assistant. changing focus does not require inventing an extra stage or altering the event.

“the session allows beginners to practise. the tutor suggested starting slowly. we look forward to meeting you.” retain who is allowed to act and the suggested cautious beginning. editing should not turn a suggestion into a compulsory instruction.
“the shop stays open until six, but the collection desk closes at four.” → collection deadline: four.
“the small room is cheaper, but we need a projector. book the equipped room.” which fact explains the choice?
“the start time is unchanged, but the room is different.” → the location changed.

“the table shows that visits fell from 80,000 in 2015 to 60,000 in 2020. they were projected in the 2025 plan to reach 90,000 by 2030.” the first “shows” describes the table; “fell” reports observations; “were projected” identifies the forecast and its source date.
“they prefer evening classes” provides a subject and finite verb completing the reason relationship.

“this travel” refers to living far from campus and commuting. “however” introduces an improvement to the problem, while “this improvement” refers to the shorter journey. “therefore” links that improvement to a possible attendance benefit. replacing it with “nevertheless” would introduce a contrast that the argument does not supply.
“tomorrow’s workshop is online, but it still starts at ten and the preparation task is unchanged.” record changed and retained details.
“used to” marks a previous arrangement; “now” gives the current arrangement.
“useful detail” is positive; “may not represent” adds a limitation.

“we will leave after the guide arrives” uses present arrives inside the future-time clause. the main clause supplies the future plan. the same pattern commonly follows when, once, until and before in this use: “i will wait until the gate opens.” do not apply this as a ban on will inside every clause with when: “i do not know when it will open” is an embedded question, not the same time-adverbial structure.

“were waiting.” musicians is plural, so use were; waiting presents the background activity. “waited outside when the caretaker arrived” is possible english but can present a different sequence rather than the requested background-in-progress meaning.

“when does registration close?” uses does+registration+base close. “please explain whether registration remains open” embeds a statement-order clause. “if places remain, students may register online” contains both a condition and the complete main clause students may register online.

“who should i contact to reserve room c?” supports an intention to arrange it, not a reservation already made. partly complete “the speaker still needs to ___ because ___.” then compare with “i received confirmation this morning” and explain the change in status.
“who work during the day” modifies adults.
